subtopic: STATEMENT ON JUDGMENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT ON PROPERTY VALUATION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON JUDGMENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT ON PROPERTY VALUATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether, now that he has had an opportunity of reading the judgment of the exchequer court concerning the expropriation of land for Malton airport, he has any further statement to make on this matter at the present time.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minisier):
subtopic: STATEMENT ON JUDGMENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT ON PROPERTY VALUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday the Leader of the Opposition asked this question:
I should like to direct to the Prime Minister a question based on reports of a judgment rendered yesterday by the exchequer court with regard to property valuation at Malton airport. Is it the intention of the Prime Minister to make a statement concerning the matter covered by this judgment, in which the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) and the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Pallett) are mentioned?
In the course of my reply I said, amongst other things:
However, I think I should say at this time that in so far as any reference to any hon. member in this house is concerned, and in particular to the hon. member for Peel, the integrity and honesty of purpose of that hon. member leaves no question in my mind.
I wish to thank the Leader of the Opposition for the support he gave me in this regard when he said:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask a supplementary question. In view of statements made in the judgment- and I am not quarrelling in any way with what the Prime Minister has said-has the Prime Minister considered referring this matter to the appropriate standing committee of the house so that it may be given the fullest and most impartial examination?
I repeat that I very much appreciated the attitude taken by the Leader of the Opposition in entirely supporting me when I said that the honesty and integrity of the hon. member left no question in my mind.
In conformity with the answer I gave, I have read carefully the judgment of the exchequer court and I have also had an opportunity of discussing the matter fully with the Minister of Transport and the hon. member for Peel. On the basis of those discussions and studies the opinion I expressed on Friday is fully confirmed. There is nothing which brings into question the integrity and honesty of the hon. member for Peel, and in so far as the minister is concerned there is, of course, no reference whatsoever throughout the entire judgment which in any way to the slightest degree suggests any impropriety.
I feel I should give some particulars regarding the suggestion that this matter might be referred to a committee. According to the judgment, which I have before me, the matters in question having to do with the valuation of land in the Malton area had their origin in the expropriation proceedings of 1954. During the period from 1954 until June 10, 1957, the hon. member for Peel acted in the capacity of solicitor with regard to this matter for some 14 or 15 veterans in that area who felt that justice was not being done to them in the offers made by the department in respect of the land expropriated.
From June, 1957-and I want to underline this-following the change of government the hon. member for Peel thereafter ceased to have any connection with the legal end, disassociating himself from that position. His endeavours were to secure what he believed to be justice for these particular constituents and veterans. It was not until January, 1959, of course, that the hon. member became chief government whip.
I carefully considered the position on the basis of an examination of that judgment and also in the light of past authorities in

Inquiries oj the Ministry respect of the submission to a committee of matters such as these concerning the privileges of any hon. member of parliament, and I found no case in which any such submission to a committee was ever provided for except where it had been alleged that there was on the part of an hon. member improper conduct resulting in his personal gain. Of that there is not one scintilla of evidence in the judgment or elsewhere as far as the hon. member for Peel is concerned.
I think I should refer to the authorities so the record will be complete in this regard. I say, first, that on the basis of the experience of the past and of the traditions of this house, all the cases referred to the standing committee on privileges and elections since 1867 had to do with alleged improper conduct whereby a member allegedly had used his public position in order to further his private interest. Those cases go back to 1877. In 1877 there was the case of a newspaper owned by Hon. T. W. Anglin, M.P. which became a party to a contract with the Post Office Department concerning the insertion of advertisements relating to the public service. However, parliament having been prorogued no action was taken by the house.
In 1890 J. C. Rykert, M.P., was charged and found guilty of having used his influence to get for one John Adams a grant of certain timber limits. This was brought before the committee and Rykert resigned his seat, having been found guilty.
In 1891 charges were brought against Hon. Thomas McGreevy, member of parliament and member of the Quebec harbours commission in connection with tenders and contracts. The committee found a conspiracy between the contractors and the member in question. A contracting firm had taken the member's brother as partner and given him an interest in the firm in order to obtain a contract. McGreevy resigned his seat.
There was the case in 1915 in which A. deW. Foster, M.P., was found by the public accounts committee to have acted as a purchasing agent for the government in the purchase of certain requirements for the army. That committee reported to the house, recommending thorough investigation and action by the Department of Justice. Before such action was taken, A. deW. Foster resigned his seat. There were four other cases of a similar nature in which the action taken resulted in the charges against the member being rejected.
That in general summarizes the situation under which the rights of parliament are subject to that jealous scrutiny which at all times must be maintained. In every case

there was moral wrongdoing or the achievement of personal gain. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, under those circumstances and reinforced by the objective attitude taken by the Leader of the Opposition when he confirmed me in the general statement I made during the course of my remarks on Friday, there is nothing to be placed before any committee.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON JUDGMENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT ON PROPERTY VALUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the Prime Minister's reply and particularly in view of his reference to myself perhaps I might be permitted to make an observation. It is quite true, as the Prime Minister has said, that I stated in the house on Friday that I had no quarrel with what the Prime Minister said on that occasion. Of course I would have no occasion either to quarrel with or support any statement the Prime Minister made on that occasion, because it was a preliminary statement pending the examination which at that time he promised to make.
Naturally I am glad to confirm what I said on that preliminary occasion. We on this side will now study the Prime Minister's very important statement today. If that statement seems to require further discussion in the house no doubt there will be an opportunity later to refer to it.
I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether he does not agree from a study of the judgment-and I had not an opportunity of making that study last Friday-that there are contradictions between statements in this judgment about a member of parliament and statements made outside the house on the same matter by the same hon. member, contradictions which in fairness to all concerned should be cleared up?

subtopic: STATEMENT ON JUDGMENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT ON PROPERTY VALUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know of no contradictions such as are suggested by the Leader of the Opposition. I may say a committee is not set up for the purpose of resolving contradictions. The circumstances under which a committee is set up are very clearly shown to be based upon a charge or charges made by a member of this house. All of us know what happens when charges are made. If charges are made, the house has the opportunity of determining whether they should be submitted to a committee. And if any hon. member makes a charge he, of course, has to substantiate that charge, and if he fails to substantiate the charge the parliamentary tradition, indeed all the experience of the past, indicates that such a member having made a charge unconfirmed

and unsupported may be himself adjudged guilty of a breach of the privileges of the house.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier, when prime minister, in the House of Commons debates of 1907, at page 5664 of Hansard, with all his regard for the traditions of parliament and the necessity of their maintenance inviolate, made this statement that is most pertinent and applicable:
The house, I hope will not depart from the sound traditions which have come to us from England and according to which there could be no inquisition into any man's conduct or standing except on charges made specifically.

subtopic: REPORTED INTENTION TO LAUNCH CANADIAN SATELLITE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REPORTED INTENTION TO LAUNCH CANADIAN SATELLITE
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister arising out of conflicting press reports, one report stating that the Prime Minister had announced at Prince Albert that a Canadian satellite would be launched in 1961, and other reports attributing to certain defence research officials that the satellite would merely be a United States satellite with certain Canadian instruments attached to it. Can the Prime Minister tell the house just what is involved, and if this is to be in fact a Canadian satellite or merely a United States satellite to be launched from a Canadian base?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REPORTED INTENTION TO LAUNCH CANADIAN SATELLITE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in so far as my statement at Prince Albert is concerned, it was in keeping with a joint announcement made in the month of April by Canada and the United States in connection with joint rocket vehicle and satellite experiments. I also dealt with the matter on another occasion.
In order to keep the record straight may I say that in so far as my remarks are concerned, and I repeat that they were in keeping with what had already been said on previous occasions, the background of the program is as follows. Canadian scientists

Inquiries of the Ministry are of the opinion that work on space research has now passed beyond the stage of hurling a satellite into space. They believe there is valuable scientific data on the properties of space that can be collected, analysed and considered.
Some time ago the defence research board and the defence research telecommunications establishment approached the appropriate United States authorities with proposals for a co-operative program of development in this field. In view of the fact that Canadian scientific personnel have the ability to make their contribution to the world's pool of knowledge in this field, we believe that Canadian technicians and scientists should be given that opportunity. They have proven themselves outstanding in conception, design and craftsmanship in the production of fine electronics components.
In so far as a satellite is concerned, the United States already has expensive and complex bases for launching earth satellites. It will be a considerable time, if ever, before it will be economic for Canada to establish her own satellite launching base. We do not believe that Canadian scientists should be held back on that account, and intend to give every possible encouragement to them to pursue this program and add to the collective pool of knowledge which can be turned to peaceful pursuits.
The purpose of launching satellites, as I have said, has now passed into the field of collecting valuable scientific data. The Canadian defence research telecommunications establishment at Shirley's bay is fully qualified to participate. When the satellite has finally been completed at D.R.T.E. it will be launched into a north-south polar orbit crossing the United States and Canada from the Vandenberg air force base in California, utilizing the multimillion dollar facilities I have already mentioned which are available there.
I mentioned that the launching would take place in 1961. I see some reference to the fact that this date has not been finally determined. The information I have received now is that it will not be launched earlier than 1961. With those explanations I think the hon. gentleman will understand the situation.

subtopic: REPORTED INTENTION TO LAUNCH CANADIAN SATELLITE
speechtext: Can the Prime Minister say how many Canadian technicians will be involved in this joint project, and whether the establishment of production facilities will result in substantial employment for Canadians? Will he also comment on the report in the press that Premier Frost has said that Moosonee is to be the launching site?

subtopic: REPORTED INTENTION TO LAUNCH CANADIAN SATELLITE
speechtext: I realize the obvious interest hon. gentlemen opposite have in the statements made by Premier Frost, but I have nothing to say with regard thereto. The general plans at the moment are that the launching will take place in the manner I have indicated. I am unable to give the hon. gentleman the details as to the numbers engaged, but I can say this. Canadians are engaged and are making a worth-while contribution to this highly desirable objective.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposilion):
subtopic: REPORTED INTENTION TO LAUNCH CANADIAN SATELLITE
speechtext: In view of what the Prime Minister has said, will he explain exactly what he meant-and I quote from the text of his statement-when he said on Saturday "a Canadian satellite is to be launched in 1961"?

subtopic: REPORTED INTENTION TO LAUNCH CANADIAN SATELLITE
speechtext: That is exactly what I meant, namely a Canadian satellite. I would call a Canadian satellite one in which the instrumentation is supplied by Canada. After all, the instrumentation is the operative part of any satellite.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Transport. In view of the congestion and still further delays on the Welland canal,

and the charge made recently that Canadian ships are being discriminated against, is the minister giving consideration to the establishment of a system of priorities in the light of what has happened in the last few days?

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY WELLAND CANAL    SUGGESTED PRIORITIES FOR CANADIAN SHIPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to be able to assure the hon. member and other members of the house that the congestion at the Welland canal has now been, for all practical purposes, overcome. At nine o'clock this morning there were only four vessels waiting to enter the canal upbound at Port Weller and only four waiting to enter down-bound at Port Colborne.
As I have said on several occasions in this house, about three weeks ago I instituted a system of partial priorities by which vessels carrying bulk commodities would alternate with package freighters. This system of priorities was discussed in my office during a session lasting about one and one half hours with the presidents of several large Canadian shipping companies and the president of the Steel Company of Canada. At the conclusion of that meeting all were eminently satisfied with the system of priorities worked out. I hope the hon. member and other members of the house feel that the steps that were taken at that time have been successful. I sincerely hope, as I know he does, that the Welland canal will be able to continue to operate satisfactorily in the future without too much delay.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY WELLAND CANAL    SUGGESTED PRIORITIES FOR CANADIAN SHIPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask a
supplementary question. In view of the minister's statement and also of the proposed visit of a convoy of United States naval ships, 32 in number, which will enter the seaway on June 26 or thereabouts, does the minister not think it desirable in the circumstances that this convoy of ships be allowed to remain in Montreal for several days rather than to go up the seaway and add to the congestion?

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY WELLAND CANAL    SUGGESTED PRIORITIES FOR CANADIAN SHIPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought the hon. member might ask this question and I therefore came prepared. I am referring now to the statement by certain people that this United States flotilla might cause a delay of three days.
I would say that this is an exaggerated statement. I may say that the number of naval ships involved is 27, not 32. If the 27 naval ships were to present themselves up-bound over a period when the canal would have been otherwise fully engaged in transiting commercial vessels, the delay would possibly be the best part of two days. I am informed that the plans of the United States navy contemplate passage of 27 ships between June 23 and June 28 inclusive.
66968-9-280i
Inquiries of the Ministry It is not possible at this date to estimate accurately the result in delay to commercial vessels if this number of naval vessels have to be passed through in addition to the commercial traffic. At present the canal is handling both upbound and downbound traffic without appreciable delays; and as I have said, at nine o'clock this morning there were only four vessels awaiting entry at Port Colborne and four at Port Weller. This is considered to be a normal situation. However, a sudden influx of naval vessels, in addition to the regular flow of commercial vessels, could quickly restore the congestion we have just overcome.
I can assure the house that steps have been taken to bring to the attention of United States authorities the serious effect on United States, Canadian and other commercial shipping which could result from the passage of this considerable number of naval vessels. I have suggested to the United States authorities that the number of vessels might be reduced without reducing the effectiveness of the display, and that the ships which do pass through the canal do so at the rate of no more than two per day in order that the least possible delay be caused to commercial shipping. I have been assured that serious; consideration is being given to my representations, and I expect an answer from the United States authorities in the course of the next few days.

subtopic: ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO IMPLEMENT PROMISES
ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO IMPLEMENT PROMISES
speechtext:
So that I may relieve members on the treasury bench of any suspense they may

have in the matter, I can say that it is my intention before I resume my seat to move an amendment which in effect will ask the house to regret the failure of the government to implement promises made before the last two elections to the people of the Atlantic provinces.
I am sure this is one occasion when even with the greatest ingenuity-and I have no doubt that the greatest ingenuity will be employed in this case-it will be very difficult for the administration to get up, when I have completed, and say, "you did not do it; why didn't you do it?" I say this because the things about which I intend to speak this afternoon are things which the hon. gentlemen opposite, particularly their leader, promised and undertook to do; and because they are promises which, except in one or two cases where I will indicate the contrary, were not made by us and were not made by the federal government before 1959.
Thus there can be no question of any obligation on the part of the Liberal party or of the former Liberal government to undertake these things. Indeed, I am not sure that many Liberals would subscribe to all the promises that were made. But whether they would or not, the fact is that they were not made by Liberals and they were not made by the Liberal government and, as I intend to show in a moment or two, with one or two exceptions they have not been carried out, either.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO IMPLEMENT PROMISES
speechtext: I wonder if I might interrupt the hon. member to ask for better attention. There seems to be more than the usual amount of competition, and I hope it will soon subside.

subtopic: ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO IMPLEMENT PROMISES
speechtext:
I appreciate your courtesy in making that suggestion to hon. members. It is not a favour which I have ever asked myself; on the whole I have been reasonably successful in securing the attention of the house, and I certainly have no complaint to make about lack of attention in respect to those things which, from time to time, I feel it expedient to say.
As I said when I began my remarks, the stock answer to every suggestion on our part that the government should do what they promised to do has been, for the past two years, "Why didn't you do it?" I pointed out that nearly all the promises to which I will refer today were promises made by the Conservative party and not by the Liberal party. It was presumably in large part by virtue of those promises that the Conservative government obtained the substantial measure of support it did succeed in getting, particularly in the second election, in the four Atlantic provinces-a majority in all the

provinces but one and, I regret to say, all the members in two of those provinces in 1958.
There is some evidence that some of the people in those provinces, perhaps a majority of them, are already beginning to have second thoughts. I should like to think they are having second thoughts because they now feel that the Liberal program which was placed before them in 1958 was so much better than the Conservative program that they should have voted for it. However, I do not flatter myself that this is the case. The view I hold is that what they are doing is what people all over the country are doing, namely judging the government, not the opposition, because it is the government which has the responsibility, having received so overwhelming a mandate, for carrying on the affairs of this country. It is not the opposition which has that responsibility, and the eyes of the country are, in my view, focussed upon the government, and it is the government which is being judged.

I might suggest to some of the hon. members who are sitting in what is usually called "the rump" that it is really a waste of time to interrupt me this afternoon, because under the rules of the house I have unlimited time, and nothing they may say will prevent me from completing what I intend to say, though it may remind me of a few additional points.
I was suggesting that this government is being judged already on the record of its performance, and while I do not regard the
Promises to Atlantic Provinces evidence of Gallup polls as infallible-the only evidence which we in this house can take as infallible in these matters is the evidence of the election itself-we do know that ever since 1943 when these Gallup polls were first taken in this country they have, on the whole, been a fairly good indication of what the vote would be in both federal and provincial elections. Hon. members will recall that in the most recent Gallup poll in the four Atlantic provinces the support which was indicated for the Progressive Conservative party by those who were asked questions was below that which it was indicated would be given to the Liberal party.
As I say, I do not attach any exaggerated importance to that, but considering the overwhelming support which was given to the party opposite in at least two of those provinces at the last election, I do think there is an indication that there is a very marked change in sentiment in that part of the country.
I have no doubt whatsoever that the government will claim credit, and very considerable credit, for two things which have happened in the Atlantic provinces since they took office. I for one will say right off, as I said when the legislation was introduced and as I have said publicly and privately ever since whenever I have had occasion to speak about it, that I give the government full credit for the special grants to the Atlantic provinces. The measure, which was brought in by the Minister of Finance in January of 1958, provided the sum of $25 million a year for a period of four years, up until the taxsharing arrangements presently provided for by law expire.
This measure was a source of considerable and very badly needed financial help to the Atlantic provinces. In the light of the experience in the past two years in those provinces I think there is not much doubt that if this action had not been taken the governments of at least some of those provinces would either have been obliged to curtail existing services to some degree or to impose additional provincial taxation. Indeed, one of the provinces, the most populous one, has proposed additional taxation in any case, though that taxation is earmarked or related to a specific and particular measure.
One of the reasons there has been the necessity for this increased financial assistance to the treasuries of these provinces is precisely the economic conditions through which the country has been passing. I do not intend to go into great detail on that subject, but I should like to give one rather striking illustration. In the month of March

Promises to Atlantic Provinces of this year the relief costs which had to be met out of the treasury of the province of Newfoundland-though, of course, half of this is reimbursed by the federal treasury under the unemployment assistance legislation-amounted to $324,884.
That may well be the peak month of the year. We certainly hope it is, but it may not be. It may be that when the figures for April are available they will be higher still, because it must be remembered that these relief costs do not immediately vanish with an increase in the level of employment in a province. As the spring advances more and more persons come to be out of work, particularly in this province where the proportion of seasonal workers is greater than the national average. There come to be more and more people out of work who have also exhausted their benefits under unemployment insurance and who are obliged therefore to resort to provincial or local relief.
There is no doubt that these costs alone have been very materially increased in all the Atlantic provinces, particularly in this last year, much more than in the year 195758, because there was a much bigger backlog of unemployment insurance benefits in 195758 than was available in this past fiscal year.
However, I come back to my original point. I want to give the government full credit for what I believe is bound to be required as long as the Atlantic provinces have a lower level of economic activity and on the whole lower incomes than the rest of the country.
I wish to turn to what I consider should be a permanent part of our federal-provincial financial arrangements, and that is some special arrangement for all the provinces and not just for the Atlantic provinces. As I pointed out to the Minister of Finance at the time of the introduction of the Atlantic grants, I think a formula should be worked out between now and 1962 that is capable of application to all the provinces and not merely to the Atlantic provinces, a formula that will be embodied in whatever may succeed the tax-sharing legislation. I do not intend to labour this point at all. I was simply making the point that I do give the government full credit for having taken this step.
I know it could be said, "Why did you not do it in 1956?" Well, I think the principal reason we did not do this in 1956 is illustrated by what we did do in 1956. We increased the payments or the abatements to the provinces under the tax-sharing arrangement from something over $500 million to substantially over $600 million over the whole country. This represented assistance of a

considerably larger amount than is represented by all the things the federal government has done in this field in the last two years. Mr. St. Laurent and Mr. Harris, in statements that were referred to by the Minister of Finance the other day, indicated quite properly that they felt, at that time, that as much of the national budget had been devoted to this field as it was felt possible to devote on that occasion.
Notwithstanding that, as the representative of a constituency in the Atlantic provinces I am very glad this government has seen fit to do more in this field. As I say, I am not criticizing it in any way, but am merely making what I think is the constructive suggestion that when it becomes a part of our regular fiscal policy, as I hope and expect it will, it will be based on a formula that could be applied, for example, to the province of Saskatchewan if it should ever find itself in conditions at all approaching those which so regrettably occasioned the original tax-sharing proposals of 20 years ago.
We hope that will never happen. We hope too

and this, of course, was pointed out by Mr. Kirk, the former member of this house for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare at the time the minister brought down this legislation-that the day will come when the level of economic activity and the level of incomes in the Atlantic provinces will be such that what are essentially deficiency payments to these provincial governments because of lower incomes in those areas will no longer be necessary. But that will be some time in coming, even if we have in the future the kind of advance in those provinces that we have had in the past 20 years, and about which I intend to say something a little later on.
The other thing for which the government will undoubtedly seek to take credit, of course, is the program for assistance in the development of thermal power and assistance in interconnections through assistance to transmission lines between the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, assistance which I am glad to note the Prime Minister offered to extend to a transmission line in the province of Newfoundland in a recent message which he sent to the premier of Newfoundland and which I understand is under very active consideration there at the present time.
About this I cannot offer the government any similar congratulations. In all but two respects this program, of course, is precisely the program that was announced by the former minister of finance in his budget in 1957, and expanded upon by the then minister

of northern affairs and national resources, Mr. Jean Lesage, in this house before the election of 1957. There were two adaptations made in this program, neither of them in my opinion advantageous to the Atlantic provinces.
I want to say a word about each of them. The first was with respect to ownership. In the original proposals made by Mr. Harris and Mr. Lesage it was suggested that the federal government should own those new facilities, those new thermal plants and those new transmission lines, but that the province should have the option to buy them at its convenience. Under the existing legislation what happens is that a loan is made to a province, a long term loan at the current borrowing rate of the government of Canada, with the usual allowances. And I make no criticism of that; but let us consider for a moment the effect of this change. Under the system we proposed the federal government could have gone ahead, if the province wanted *-and, of course, we could do nothing under either scheme unless a province wanted-with thermal plants and even with transmission lines somewhat in advance of the demand for the power, and the federal treasury would for that period, until the demand caught up, have carried that burden. It would have been some burden upon the federal treasury; we knew that. We intended that, we proposed that, when the original scheme was put before parliament.
Under the present scheme the province must start paying interest on the loan and start amortizing the loan immediately. So there would have to be, in view of the much more restricted financial base that each of those provinces has, if you like more prudence; but I would rather put it this way. There has to be a real certainty of an almost immediate demand for the power or it is not going to be developed. What we were suggesting was that we should go a little ahead of the demand, provide the additional power and have it there as an attraction, as a sort of magnet for the development of users of the power.
Of course if the level of economic activity that existed in 1956 and early 1957 had continued that would not have been a problem, because it was quite clear that if the curve of demand was going to continue at the rate it then was going on there would be no doubt about the demand, but we have seen that these things can change very quickly. We have seen, for example, that in the case of Beechwood, which the government of New Brunswick considered was very necessary to that province and very urgently needed, they have found it necessary to export some of this power to the United States.

I now come to the other two points of this second clause. The second one is that crown corporations are to be established in the area. There may have been crown corporations established in the area, but if there are, apart from the extension to the area of the

Northern Canada Power Corporation or whatever the name of it is which was in existence before that time, and I think it was even designated for the purpose by the previous administration, I am not aware of any other federal crown corporations that have been established for the purpose of promoting the decentralization of industry in the Atlantic provinces. If there have been such crown corporations established and I have overlooked them, and if any member of the government points them out, I shall certainly be glad to make a rectification.
The third point is that special fiscal consideration be given to private enterprise which will encourage the location of industry in the Atlantic area and further encourage the processing of our natural resources. I presume that means fiscal considerations given in the Atlantic area that were not going to be given in other parts of the country. I know of no such considerations. Indeed, far from having any fiscal considerations in this field, we have had fiscal "deconsideration" if I may coin a word, because of the necessity under which the government has found itself to increase the corporation tax in order to attempt to fill part of the vacuum in the treasury. In addition, of course, the legislation which is now before a committee of this house to increase the charges upon employers and employees under the Unemployment Insurance Act will not have the effect of promoting industrial development either in the Atlantic provinces or anywhere else.

It was given by Mr. St. Laurent before the election because Mr. St. Laurent, as the hon. member knows, never attempted to conceal even unfavourable things or things that might be unfavourable in a particular locality, and it was all the more credit to him, in my opinion.
I should now like to draw attention to certain other supplementary statements that were made in the elections of 1957 and 1958 that seem to me to relate fairly directly to these two points. I have not finished with this document yet but I should like to deal with the natural resources program and the decentralization of industry. I have not paid much attention to what was said in those elections by anyone except the Prime Minister, simply because I did not think it would be fair to take too much of the time of the house in dealing with them, even though my time is not limited. I should now like to draw attention to the statement made by the Prime Minister at Cambridge, Nova Scotia on June 3, 1957 as reported in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of June 4 of that year. According to this report in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald the Prime Minister said:
The federal government had overtaxed the people by $500 million last year, he said, and this would likely be increased to $700 million this year "if they remain in office". Mr. Diefenbaker said his party advocated "equal opportunity for all Canadians".
I will read on:
In Nova Scotia, he said, the average personal income had decreased 5.9 per cent from $886 in 1948 to $815 in 1955. The Canadian average personal income increased during the same period from $1 025' to $1,078.
I presume the Prime Minister verified those statements. I have not attempted to do so. He went on to give similar figures, for Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. Then the press report continues:
Mr. Diefenbaker advocated a national development program encompassing decentralization of

Promises to Atlantic Provinces industry which, he said, would help Nova Scotia to keep her sons and daughters at home.
No details, of course, were given in that report. Then on April 29 at Charlottetown as reported in a Canadian Press report in the Ottawa Journal, of April 30, we find these words:
If some of the economic conditions in the mari-times existed in western Canada, members of parliament from the west would soon let the country know about it.
That is the Prime Minister. To continue:
He could not understand how the maritimes time after time elected Liberal members "who make their greatest contribution in the silence they preserve".
A moral can be drawn from that, which I will leave the hon. members on the other side of the house from the maritime provinces to draw for themselves. Then, I continue quoting from this article:
And at Charlottetown (the above had been said at Summerside) with the province's four Conservative candidates on the platform behind him, he added: "You people in Prince Edward Island want action. Then, send these four candidates to the House of Commons. We'll give you action."
I believe the people of Prince Edward Island, with the exception, of course, of the Atlantic provinces grants which were very acceptable and which were made before the second election, would be interested in what the additional action has been.
Then, at St. Stephen-this is from the Saint John Telegraph-Journal of May 4, the Prime Minister is reported to have said on May 3:
At St. Stephen, Mr. Diefenbaker spoke of maritime rights and said the eastern provinces should not be "back-benchers in a confederation of equals".
The Conservative party had made confederation possible. If elected, it would work out with the provinces a new deal that would remove the "inequities that too long have held back the maritime provinces".
Then, he quotes the same figures again for income and he added:
"That's a challenge which should demand action."
I might say I took this particular quotation from St. Stephen because at Milltown, which is immediately adjacent to St. Stephen, there was at that time a textile plant which was in operation. The last thing I heard about that textile plant was in February when I was in Fredericton, and the machinery had been sold to someone in the Dominican Republic.

This was said at Campbellton. Well, what about raw materials-

Perhaps the hon. gentleman would allow me to continue and I would be delighted to answer his question in a moment. In that area, at Campbellton and in the Bathurst area, as hon. members know, unhappily the very considerable minerals discovered there are not being exploited at the present time. I read some of the reports of the Iron Ore Company and the other companies mining in Labrador and Ungava and they claim that their exports of iron ore are increasing.
Then, here is another quotation from the same place, and this is in direct quotes:
We in this party have launched in every part of this country a national development plan, and the purpose that we have in mind is to assure that your sons and daughters may remain within this province, instead of being forced by economic necessity to leave for other parts of Canada or the United States.
Everyone would like to see that, of course, but the fact is that what has happened does not correspond with what was hoped for.

Then again at Campbellton, in that same speech, and this is in direct quotes:
In order to persuade business firms it is to their advantage to process our raw materials here in Canada, we must show them by tact and other inducements that they will save money by processing those materials in Canada. I say this to you: If we form a government we will introduce legislation which will provide such inducements for we intend to see that Canada shall become the great industrial nation which her raw materials make possible.
We have not seen this legislation. Then, the Montreal chamber of commerce were told on February 19, 1957, and this was about inflation and tight money, by the Prime Minister:
The dread problem of inflation will not be met by regulations which while effective against the individual permit government to have and enjoy the sole privilege of contributing to inflationary pressures.
Then, there is this:
Federal government expenditures constitute the biggest inflationary factor in our economy.
Federal government expenditures are very considerably more today than they were when that speech was made.
Then, at Truro on May 1, as reported in the Globe and Mail for the following day, the Prime Minister said about this tight money policy:
Through its tight money policy, he added, the government has throttled the capital investment which maintains economic growth, supports welfare expenditures and provides full employment.
Small and medium businessmen, farmers and fishermen have been squeezed and even forced into bankruptcy by government policy, he added. "We contend and have contended that this is economically unsound", he said.
As a result, he added, provincial governments and school administrations have had to pay excessive interest rates to finance vital public works and improvements. There has been regional discrimination, Mr. Diefenbaker charged, in the distribution of available credit with the maritimes and western provinces bearing the brunt of this inequality.
I think in the maritimes, the western provinces and everywhere else today there is no provincial government, no school administration, that can borrow money at the interest rates which were prevailing in February of 1957. If these things were going to be remedied, the remedy has been worse than the disease.
There is another report of the same speech at Truro, and this is from the Halifax Chronicle-Herald:
The little man-the farmer, the fisherman and the small businessman-is being crushed by the Liberal government's tight money policy, John G. Diefenbaker, national leader of the Progressive Conservative party, said here Wednesday night. The real causes of inflation in this country are over-spending by the federal government and too-high taxes, he said.
Promises to Atlantic Provinces
Then, at Cambridge, Nova Scotia, on June 3, 1957:
Unemployment in Canada had reached the 300,000 mark because of the tight-money policy, he said.
He said that the tight-money policy had struck a "hard body blow" at small business in Canada and he promised that a Progressive Conservative government would bring into operation a policy whereby a loan fund would be available at low interest "so that small business won't be driven out by larger groups".
Well, where is it?
Then in the second election, in 1958, the Prime Minister made one or two references to interest rates. At that time interest rates were not as high as they were in 1957. In Calgary, according to the Winnipeg Tribune of March 15, the Prime Minister claimed the day before
-that interest rates had fallen sharply as a result of government action since last June from a high of 4.33 per cent to 2.89 per cent in recent weeks.
When they fall, of course, it is the result of government policy. But when, as has happened almost all the time since the conversion loan, they rise, then it is the fault of the Americans or of businessmen who are borrowing money from the chartered banks -the fault of everyone except the government. There were several similar references during the 1958 election campaign.
I should like to make one other reference to the topic of small business. In the election of 1957, speaking of the need for assistance to small business, the Prime Minister was reported as follows in the Campbellton rally of May 4:
We Intend, as well, to do something to assist small businessmen in this country. They find themselves today caught, irretrievably caught, in a situation whereby they cannot survive. We believe the time has come to provide very much after the fashion of the federal government in the United States, assistance to small business, to enable the backbone of our national business, the small businessman, to survive and to prosper.
And even in the election of 1958 something was said on this subject. At Summerside on February 27, as reported in the Charlottetown Guardian of the following day, the Prime Minister announced:
-that if his government is re-elected it is their intention at the first session of parliament to give consideration to a system whereby small business may be able to expand on reasonable terms, and have available to it a system of financing which is being considered to enable small business to meet its responsibility in expanding and assuring extra jobs. A community will continue to prosper and expand if small business expands, he said.
And a very similar statement was made at Yarmouth on March 26. So much for the first two of those resolutions. The third had reference to the power development, and I have already dealt with it. The fourth had reference to transportation and this is what the

Promises to Atlantic Provinces Conservative candidates pledged themselves to do about transportation:
We are committed to the original pledge given to our people at the time of confederation that freight rates would be adjusted and transportation facilities would be provided so that our geographic position would not prejudice our producers in having reasonable access to the markets of Canada.
I could go on and make several references to statements made by the Prime Minister on this subject which are in much the same vein, but I see that I am taking an inordinate amount of time. It seems to me that this is a very clear statement of what the electors were led to expect from a Conservative government. But what has happened? What has happened is that freight rates have gone up. Freight rates have not been adjusted so as to give maritime producers greater access to the markets of central Canada; the exact reverse has been the case. It is true that some small amelioration of the increase has been made by this parliament at this session or, at least, it has been provided for-* precisely how it is going to be made is not yet very clear. But the fact is that these rates are higher and, certainly, the transportation facilities are in no way improved compared with what they were before this statement was made.
Then there were also some specific pledges made particularly about the Chignecto canal and about the Newfoundland railway which I do not intend to deal with at this time.
Then the next item in what I call the Atlantic charter of the Tory party is the capital projects program. Here is the promise:
We favour the immediate institution of an Atlantic capital projects program which will provide federal capital assistance for provincial projects designed to enlarge the basic economy of the area.
That is a great hope, but all it is is a hope. We have heard nothing about it since. Certainly, we have heard nothing about it in this parliament.
Then there is another promise, the one concerning the Canadian coastguard. "We shall press", members of the Conservative party said, "for a Canadian coastguard". At this point I think I should also make one reference to what the Prime Minister himself had to say about this question in 1957 because I want to make it clear that the Prime Minister was committed on this point. At Cambridge, Nova Scotia, on June 3, he is reported in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald the next day as follows:
Mr. Diefenbaker also advocated a Canadian coastguard service to assure that marine disasters were kept at a minimum.
A similar statement was made at Lunenburg later the same day.
We know the history of the coastguard. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees), when

he was first asked about this after the election, came into the house and read verbatim a statement which had been made by his predecessor, the same statement which, I think, was originally made by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) about the service which we now have. No change whatever has been made in that situation, and no explanation or apology has been offered for the total failure to do anything to implement this particular specific promise.
The seventh of these points has to do with the fiscal needs of the Atlantic provinces. I had something to say on this subject at the beginning of my speech and I need not repeat that again.
I wish to say something about the coal situation in the Atlantic provinces. I do not need to say anything further about coal in relation to power development, because I have already dealt with that question. But promises were made that the production of coal would be increased, and the bitterest and most unfair and distorted criticism was expressed of Mr. St. Laurent because of a statement he made at Fredericton during that election campaign in which he said that in his view the value of coal for purposes other than as fuel was such that he would not take the responsibility for expenditure to increase the production of coal. But Mr. St. Laurent also said that no one wanted to see coal mining towns become ghost towns any more than anyone wanted to see the gold mining towns of northern Quebec and northern Ontario become ghost towns, and that steps must be taken to maintain existing production. The Conservative party, on the other hand, took the view that production should be increased, and gave an undertaking accordingly. I suggest, in the light of the prospects for markets, that that was a wholly irresponsible attitude to have taken. At the same time it was suggested that because Mr. St. Laurent had stated he could do nothing to increase coal production he had suggested that existing production would be curtailed, whereas the whole tenor of his speech was in the opposite direction.

We have in mind to provide for the fisherman, legislation similar to that provided for agriculture. Under the latter program, he said, a floor price was decided in relation to the farmer's costs.

Of course, nothing of that kind has been forthcoming. Not only that, but in view of the failure of the fisheries in some parts of the Atlantic provinces and particularly on the northeast coast of Newfoundland last season it is regrettable that nothing happens when other ameliorative steps are suggested.
In many ways, of course, the gravest situation of all is that which has resulted in the Atlantic provinces because of the disproportionate incidence of unemployment in those provinces.
In the same speech in Charlottetown to which I have already referred and on many other occasions throughout the country is recorded the Prime Minister's most definite pledge of all. This has been placed on the record on several occasions but I do not apologize for putting it on again. This is to be found in the Toronto Star of February 28, reporting on a speech made in Charlottetown.
"I will make one more promise," the Prime Minister asserted. "I make this promise. My pledge is to every man and woman in this nation who is unemployed. So long as I am Prime Minister no one will be allowed to suffer in this nation."
The latest figures, I think, speak for themselves and are very eloquent. The latest figures, as produced in the release on the unemployment situation for the month of April, which were released on May 20 last, for Canada as a whole show that while in March the unemployment was 8.6 per cent of the labour force;-and these are the lower, or
D.B.S. figures, not the very much higher figures in the listings of persons actually seeking work-in April, 1958 they were 8.62 per cent. In April, 1959 we were very gratified that it was only 7.3 per cent. That is still a very high level of unemployment for the nation as a whole. But when you compare the national figure with the figure for Newfoundland, which on April 19, 1958 was 24.07 per cent, and April, 1959, 28.2 per cent, there is not much ground for feeling very optimistic. When you take the three maritime provinces you find it was 16.93 per cent in April, 1958 and it is still 12 per cent. There is not much ground for optimism. These figures, of course, are very much higher than they are in Ontario; higher still than they are in the prairie provinces where the unemployment is the lowest in the country, or even in British Columbia. Quebec, of course, comes fairly close to the maritime figure.
There is no doubt that if at the present time we had on a national basis unemployment at the level it is in the four Atlantic provinces today it would be a major calamity to this country, and for that area it is a very serious thing. To a great extent at least the

suffering is ameliorated because that area is part of the national economy and it enjoys the advantages of the national social security and other national welfare benefits. They do not provide employment but they do at least take away some of the rigors of unemployment that were felt 25 years ago; nevertheless, it is a serious situation that calls for serious action. I should like to commend to the government, before I conclude what I have to say, the series of editorials which appeared in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, an independent newspaper, entitled, "A Blueprint For Atlantic Advance". I am not going to take the time of the house to read them or even to quote from them; I just draw them to the attention of hon. members. I think all hon. members have probably at one time or another received a copy-certainly, all of us from the Atlantic provinces, I am sure, have- containing some very valuable suggestions for action which, it seems to me, should be considered, not in the way in which this government so often considers problems but with a view to early action.
Now, sir, having taken rather longer than I had intended to take, I shall conclude by moving, seconded by the hon. member for Kent, New Brunswick (Mr. Michaud);
That all the words after the word "that" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
this house regrets the failure of the government to keep its election promises to the people of the Atlantic provinces, and regrets further its failure to take measures to strengthen, in the light of acute unemployment in the area, the basic economy of the Atlantic provinces.

No other government made such promises. What of the statement made by the late lamented personal friend of mine and of us all, Hon. Angus L. My hon. friend talks about promises!

Promises to Atlantic Provinces

speechtext:
Yes, very successfully, indeed, after we drew attention to the fact that she could not operate until they put in the engines.
The solicitude of the hon. member for the maritimes is really touching; it is just touching. I remember how he always used to respond so sympathetically, when he sat on this side of the house, to the arguments which we advanced on behalf of the maritimes. You could see the gleam in his eye; you could see the approbation. I am sure that he must have urged his colleagues to do some of the things which he talked about this afternoon but apparently he was unable to convince them.
He regrets the low standard of the economy. He referred to unemployment in the maritime provinces. He said that if the same degree of unemployment prevailed in the nation as a whole it would be a national disaster. I think, Mr. Speaker, that there is some justification for such a statement if the figures that the hon. member gave are correct. I have no doubt that he checked them but, after all, they deal with seasonal unemployment there. Lumbering operations have stopped. There is a great deal of unemployment in the fishing industry at the moment and these figures are not representative of industrial unemployment whatsoever in this nation.
I should like to draw to his attention something that originated with the dominion bureau of statistics. I have not got their publication, to tell the hon. gentleman the truth, but he quoted with approbation a few moments ago an editorial from the Halifax Chronicle-Herald and I can tell him that this statement is reproduced in an editorial in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald of today.
The employment expansion in the Atlantic region was greater from March to April this year than in the same period of the last three years. In April an estimated 459,000 persons had jobs, about 18,000 more than in March and 24,000 more than a year ago.
I think that disposes of the hon. member's argument. In addition, Macleans Building Reports has a rather interesting commentary. These provinces which are so poverty stricken, these provinces which have been so grossly betrayed by this government, these provinces which have sunk to such a hopeless level, according to the dire and gloomy statements of the hon. gentleman, what is their record with respect to building? In Canada as a whole for the first five months of this year construction is down below the level of last year but in the Atlantic region there is a gain of 9.6 per cent this year compared with last year, the largest gain in any area in the Dominion of Canada. In the Atlantic
[Mr. Pickersgill.l

area nearly $100 million has been applied for by way of loans for construction within the first five months of this year.
Of course the economic situation there is not as good as one would like to see it. One never is satisfied. We are looking forward, we are hoping and planning and we intend to make progress day after day and year after year. We have made and are making substantial progress in the maritime provinces and the figures to which I have referred at least bear that out. The hon. member referred to the platform on which we agreed and I must express my appreciation for his compliment on the draftmanship of some of us who were present at those Atlantic conferences. He also paid the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) a great compliment by reading at great length extracts from speeches made by him in various parts of the maritime provinces. I had the pleasure of hearing him at the meeting in Cambridge in my own constituency, at Halifax and at the wind-up meeting of the campaign in Sydney. I can vouch for the fact that the Prime Minister made these statements. I can vouch for the fact that he intended them to be believed. I vouch for the fact that the Prime Minister and the government are carrying out the pledges which were made at that time.
This government has been in power for two years and during that time an election and an economic recession have intervened. We do not pretend to be supermen. We do not pretend to be able to achieve miracles. We do not pretend that we are perfect. But we do say that in the two years we have been in office we have done more for the maritime provinces, for the Atlantic area, than the former government did in at least the preceding 25 years. The hon. gentleman could not help himself, of course, but he was good enough to give us credit for the maritime adjustment grants which we introduced at the first session after we came into office whereby the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Newfoundland each receives $7,500,000 as a special adjustment grant and the province of Prince Edward Island receives $2,500,000, a total of $25 million, this to last during the currency of the dominion-provincial agreements.
These adjustment grants were sought from the preceding government for years. The maritime premiers representing all the maritime provinces made pleas for these or comparable grants and every time they were turned down. They were coldly rebuffed because it was taken for granted that the people of the maritime provinces, having voted Liberal for so many years, would continue to do so and therefore they did not have to pay any attention to their pleas and

they just took them for granted. It was not until, as I said, the handwriting was seen on the wall that the previous government attempted to deal with the situation at all.
My hon. friend has gone to some length this afternoon to prove that the coal subvention policy inaugurated by this government for the development of thermal power within the maritime provinces was the same scheme as was proposed by the preceding government and particularly by the Hon. Mr. Winters and the Hon. Mr. Harris. I say categorically, without going into the details, that there is practically no similarity between the two programs whatsoever. One was a deathbed repentance brought about on the eve of an election whereby the former government saw that they would have to do something. They did not know what they should do. They had not given any consideration to the problem and apparently did not have anyone to advise them very well. As a result they came up wtih some sort of crackbrained scheme which would not have worked. The proof that it would not have worked is to be found in the fact that the provincial governments of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island-I believe I am correct with respect to Prince Edward Island-said that the scheme would not work and they would not accept it.
We campaigned in May and June of 1957 primarily on the thermal scheme. That was the main matter which we discussed. At that time we said that their plan would not work because the plants were to be owned by the federal government. I noticed that my hon. friend was a little bit vague this afternoon and said that somehow they could be transferred to the provincial government.

subtopic: ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO IMPLEMENT PROMISES
speechtext: I am sure the minister does not want to be unfair.

subtopic: ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO IMPLEMENT PROMISES
speechtext: I certainly do not.

subtopic: ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO IMPLEMENT PROMISES
speechtext: I was very precise about it. I said they were to be owned in the first instance by the federal government with an option to purchase by the provinces.

subtopic: ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO IMPLEMENT PROMISES
speechtext:
What the option to purchase was was one of the terms which was always in dispute because there was correspondence, as my hon. friend knows, and telegrams between the premiers of the two provinces and the responsible officers here as to the definition of those terms. There was no satisfactory definition as far as the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick were concerned. Our proposition was that these plants would be built by the federal government and sold outright to the provinces so that we would have a centralized operation instead of the Northern Power Corporation coming in and
Promises to Atlantic Provinces operating the power plant in one place and the province operating the plant in another place, which we said was absolutely impractical and impossible.
As to the question of the use of coal, the former government's proposal was that coal should be provided, as I recall it, so that energy could be produced at cost. There was no definition of "cost" and none was ever suggested. Mr. St. Laurent said that whatever the cost was that was the cost that would have to be paid for power. As has been pointed out by the Prime Minister and by every hon. member from Nova Scotia who came here in 1957, as was pointed out by the premier of Nova Scotia, that was absolutely ridiculous. Unless there was some definition of "cost" how could it be known whether there would be any benefit to the province? It might be that the costs would be far greater than we were paying and no purpose would be served whatsoever by the federal government building these plants or transmission lines. In the proposals submitted by this party the matter of "costs" was determined. It was agreed that a subvention would be paid so as to permit the coal to be competitive with coal landed in Ontario and reduce the cost of power to what we thought would be a price competitive with that for power produced by coal in other parts of Canada. Those were two of the major differences between the two schemes.
Of course one might say that this is political but it is not an effective answer. All of these matters were raised during the 1957 campaign. The claims pro and con were made by the respective parties, the Liberals saying theirs was better. They never said it was identical with ours. We were saying that we had something that was different and that was better. What happened? On election day ten out of twelve members supporting the scheme advocated or supported by the premier of Nova Scotia and advocated by this party were elected and only two of the hon. gentlemen supporting the other scheme were elected. Then six months later those two fell by the wayside and 12 members were elected to this house. That is the judgment of the people of Nova Scotia as to the relative merits of the two schemes.
I must say this. My hon. friend also, in dealing with the statement made at Fredericton by the then prime minister, had something to say about it. He has the same difficulty, although he smoothed it over, that they had in trying to explain it to the electors and as did a colleague of his, the minister of public works at that time from Nova Scotia, who attempted to explain the speech on the platform in Nova Scotia, failed and quit trying to give any answer at all

Promises to Atlantic Provinces because he said it was not understood. That was the only explanation that was given. Certainly no one else ever understood it and it has not been understood today either. Certainly the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate understands it less than does anybody else. At any rate, if you accept that speech at its face value, the coal would still be under the ground under any circumstances.
Something has been said about coal. Perhaps I should say a word about coal right now. I did not want to interrupt my hon. friend because I have interrupted him several times. He stated that in the election we promised that we would increase the sale of coal. There is no doubt that we promised subventions.

subtopic: ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO IMPLEMENT PROMISES
speechtext: To increase the production of coal.

subtopic: ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO IMPLEMENT PROMISES
speechtext:
To increase the production of coal. There is no doubt that we made a promise with respect to subventions on the movement of coal in the maritime provinces and I stand by that promise. I do not recall -although I do not deny it; I should like to see the record-that any specific promises were made with respect to an over-all increase in the production of coal or the consumption of coal as compared with those areas. But this is something of what we have done in so far as coal is concerned. When we came into office we increased the preference on Canadian coal for use in dominion public buildings so that coal would get a preference of 20 per cent in competitive bidding against other coals. As a result of that preference it is estimated by the department that the increased consumption of Canadian coal amounted to over 200,000 tons a year. We have paid out money already on this thermal scheme to which the hon. gentleman referred. It is not something that is going to be done in the future; it was not something that was going to be done when the province requested that it be done. I can assure you that, in my opinion, the province would never have requested this federal government or any federal government to carry out the scheme which they proposed at that time. Hence the scheme would not have been in being at this time.
This government has paid subventions on the movement of coal within the maritime provinces, a matter to which the hon. gentleman referred dubiously. He rather questioned the accuracy of the Prime Minister's report. The Prime Minister was dealing with specific and definite suggestions for the use of thermal plants in the maritime provinces to generate power for industrial use. Since we got the scheme into operation we have paid out over $1,692,933 in subventions on the movement

of coal in the maritime provinces for thermal plants there. That subvention is used to reduce the cost of power not to the householder but to industrial plants only so that we can assist in the development of industry. All of that benefit has been passed on for industrial development within the maritime provinces. I may have a word or two to say on that matter a little later on. That of course, was an entirely new subject but it was something which we promised. We said that if we were elected we would inaugurate this dual system of assisting in the building of thermal plants and transmission lines in the maritime provinces. That has been extended to Newfoundland as well. That was one phase of it.
The other phase was that we would pay subventions on the movement of coal in the maritime provinces to service these plants so that the benefit would be passed on to the industrial consumer. As I said, on that subvention alone we have paid out over $1,692,000. As to the movement of coal, there is no doubt, as the hon. gentleman said, that coal production suffered in this country. I want to point out to him this fact, although he undoubtedly knows it. Coal production has suffered in every coal producing area in the world as far as I know, certainly in the western world or the free world. The degree of unemployment here, bad as it is, has been less than elsewhere. To any man who is unemployed even for a day, it is a serious thing to him. To be unemployed for 40 days is an extremely serious thing. There have been miners who have been unemployed for a period of 40 days in the maritime coal fields. I think all of that is over. There may be a few of those left in one or two pits. But had it not been for the subsidy policy which this government inaugurated and put into effect the degree of unemployment would have been double or treble what it has been during this year. As I said-and I want this to be understood-the degree of unemployment in the past year in the Nova Scotia coal field has been less than the degree of unemployment in any other coal field in the western world- and the figures to prove that are there from the dominion coal board. Whether you take as an example Germany, Britain, Virginia, Pennsylvania or wherever you go, the number of men employed two years ago, the increase of unemployment is greater in every other coal field in the world. That is not a mere accident, Mr. Speaker. That fact is in part at least-and in substantial part-owing to the generous subsidy provisions which this government put into effect in order to maintain a high degree of employment in these Nova Scotia coal fields and so that the Canadian

product was upheld and its place was not taken entirely by coal imported from the United States.
Last year, the fiscal year ended in March 31, we moved 425,928 tons or in round figures
426,000	tons of coal into Ontario-despite a drop in industrial demand, despite a tremendous fall off in United States imports-at a cost of $1,938,000. It is the first time Canadian coal moved into Ontario in any appreciable quantity since before the war or since about 1937 or 1938. This government, by a subsidy policy has brought Nova Scotia coal back into the markets of Ontario, as I said at a substantial cost. This coming year, the year ending March 31 next, it is estimated that we will move into Ontario alone 850,000 tons of coal as compared with 450,000 tons last year or twice as much and the total cost of that movement will be over $12 million for the entire subsidy program, or $4,300,000 more than we paid out last year. Yet my hon. friends ask what we have done for the maritime provinces.
In the past, when we have been suffering from recession, when we have not had surpluses but have had deficits, we have gone ahead with our social security measures and have done everything that this government has done. We are also providing 50 per cent more for the movement of our coal from the mari-times to Ontario than was ever provided by our predecessors. Of course, we also established a new principle in connection with it. The Nova Scotia government is acting in partnership with us and to the extent of 20 per cent of the increased subsidy to a maximum of $500,000 the Nova Scotia government will co-operate.
Mr. Speaker, one could go on to speak at length on the coal matter, but I do not think it is necessary. I think the record of this government is clear in so far as coal is concerned. Despite the unfortunate period in which we have been operating, despite the shrinkage in demand, the industrial recession and everything else, I think it is clear that we have established here a record of which any government could be properly proud and of which the people in the coal mining areas of Nova Scotia, the maritimes and Cape Breton are appreciative. Make no mistake about that. The situation is one which is giving and will continue to give this government concern because we want to see the coal industry put on a firm basis. We want to see employment maintained there.
My hon. friend made some remarks,-I do not want to be unkind and I do not want to say sneering remarks-light remarks, about the fact we were taking the same attitude toward this problem as we were taking
8, 1959
Promises to Atlantic Provinces toward other serious problems. Here is a news story in the Cape Breton Post Record which is headed, "No More Idle Time". Then, underneath that heading there are the words, "Government praised". This news story reads in part as follows:
Because of increased government subventions, there will be no more idle times this year in Nova Scotia coal mines, after June, district vice-president Stephen Delhanty told the regular session of the Princess local of the united mine workers of America Saturday night.
He highly commended the federal government along with the provincial government of Nova Scotia for coming forward with assistance, without which there would be a great deal more distress in the coal industry in this province.
I could go on reading that laudatory article for quite a few minutes, Mr. Speaker, but this is a case where repetition is not necessary. The facts are so obvious they speak for themselves, and there is no necessity for repeating them.

speechtext:
Before the minister goes on to another subject, perhaps he will permit a question. Did I understand the minister to say, as I think he did, that he did not recall any promise made by his party before the election of 1957 to increase coal production? I have here an advertisement published by his party which contains this sentence:
Your Progressive Conservative candidates are in favour of a policy that will increase coal production.

subtopic: ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO IMPLEMENT PROMISES
speechtext:
We were certainly in favour of it and we supported a policy which has increased and will continue to increase substantially the demand for coal in the thermal plants of the Atlantic provinces. As I pointed out here a moment ago, the answer to that is that last year we increased the market in Ontario from 450,000 tons to 510,000 tons and we hope to increase it this year to 850,000 tons.
My hon. friend made some reference to the fact that we were going to refer this matter to a royal commission. He infers that this is a delaying procedure. I have already answered that. If there is any delaying procedure in what we have done in the last two years, in the accomplishments we have attained, then the miners of Nova Scotia will pray for more and more delay, and a continuance of it. Make no mistake about that.
We also realize that the coal industry is in a critical condition. There are problems facing that industry which have to be solved, and this is true all over the world. The competing fuels, gas and oil, as well as the possibility of atomic energy which is on the horizon, create a situation which deserves the most careful study, not simply the short term planning that we have had to do, frankly, since we came into power. We have been

Promises to Atlantic Provinces faced with one crisis after another, and the preceding government did nothing whatever to alleviate this problem. We did work out an interim solution, and we are continuing to do that. We want also, however, to arrive at a long term solution so that maximum employment can be provided in the coal fields.
It is because we are trying to make a long term study of the problems of that industry, and not because we are trying to sweep them under the carpet where our opponents left them, that we intend to refer this matter to a commission or some other body for study and report. Then, we shall arrive not only at the short term solution, as we have done, but also a long term solution, which will work in concert in the years to come.
My hon. friend read the catalogue from A to Z, as I have said, and referred to every speech the Prime Minister made, to all the advertisements that were published, and as I have said this points up the fact that we did have a positive program to put before the people. I do not intend to follow him on all the matters with which he dealt. He referred to transportation. It is true that we are suffering from a transportation problem. I wonder who would expect us to satisfactorily solve the transportation problem of the maritime provinces or in fact any area, but particularly the maritimes and the far west, in two years? I would think hon. gentlemen opposite would be amongst the last to deal with transportation, and reflect upon it, after having failed to deal with it during their term of office. As I recall it, the Turgeon commission was set up under the regime of the preceding government. If I recall it, the Turgeon commission made certain recommendations with respect to horizontal increases. They deprecated them and suggested that some alternative should be found.
When was that report, Mr. Speaker? My hon. friend at least has the advantage of knowing the subject on which he is going to speak, but we have to answer as we stand here, without any preparation and without any material in front of us. My own impression is that the Turgeon commission report was somewhere around the early fifties, 1951 or 1952. What has been done since 1952? We still have horizontal increases piled one upon the other, with all their detrimental effects.
