As I said, my hon. friend is also now going back into what was said by us several years ago. This is a compliment. As I said, we have not accomplished everything that we set out to do because there were so many things left undone by the preceding government it is going to take us some time. I do not want to prophesy, but I doubt very much if we could accomplish everything that should be done in the first four years. We have taken steps in connection with the problem referred to by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill)- his reference was lengthy and possibly exaggerated-that is, the incidence of freight rates upon the east and the west. This is a temporary thing because it will not cure the disease from which the people in the east and in the west are suffering, namely, high freight rates. The people of the Atlantic area have a claim on the people in other areas of Canada. In the first place, they have made a very great contribution to our very form of government in other parts of Canada; they have supplied many of the leaders in the fields of education, industry and of government in other areas of Canada. They played a large part in the early years in the development of other areas; and, therefore, when they now ask that they not be left behind

they are merely asking that we begin to recognize the sacrifices and the contributions that they have made in the years gone by so that other areas of Canada might be opened up and developed. It is for this reason that they are not very excited about the prospect of opening up of the north. They feel, and I believe rightly so, that the raising of the levels of incomes of maritimers ought at least to have priority over the opening of yet another vast new area in Canada. They feel that they have not yet received adequate compensation for the opening up of western Canada.
The policies of the government in regard to the Atlantic area in the main, outside of the items listed by the minister, have been a continuation of a policy of neglect and a policy of procrastination. I notice in a news release, a Canadian Press dispatch of January 6, 1959, where:
Alvin Hamilton, federal minister of national resources, said Monday the government has plans to revitalize Alberta's coal industry.
He said the government is expected to announce further details of the plan during the next session of parliament.
We have not heard of those plans as yet. However, if the minister has very extensive plans in mind, whereby he hopes to revitalize that enterprise in Alberta, I am sure that those who have an interest in mining in the maritimes would also like to see him announce a plan whereby their enterprise might be revitalized.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose for the dinner recess I was emphasizing the fact that we owe much to those who live in the Atlantic provinces. Our leaders of the past and many of our leaders of the present were raised and educated in the Atlantic areas. The expense of the opening up of the rest of the dominion was to a great extent absorbed by those who now live in the Atlantic provinces. As Canadians they have rights. They are not asking for any hand-outs. I have noted with interest how at meetings of dominion-provincial premiers even such men as the premier of British Columbia and the premier of Saskatchewan have asked that the federal government do all within its power to help those in the Atlantic area. I, along with the Minister of National Revenue, realize that helping the Atlantic provinces is going to take a great deal of money, a great deal of energy and a great deal of imagination on the part of the government of the day so that the time may arrive when those living in the Atlantic area will have their economy restored to the point where their people can also have equal chances with us in the field of personal income, education, health and all the other matters that all of us are desirous of having. This requires a new deal as the Prime Minister indicated at election time, it calls for a time of greatness, not little bits and little pieces. It does not call for neglect or for procrastination so that, in the words of the Minister of National Revenue, the Conservatives might win two or three more times yet. It needs action now. The time of needed greatness that was mentioned is now.
It has often been mentioned that the resources of the Atlantic area are limited. Even if that were so we would be able to point to the people of Norway who, with their limited resources, have been able to achieve a standard of living that is almost unequalled in the western world. However, it is our contention that the resources are available. I indicated that we might well embark on a program of smelting the iron ore that is available in Labrador and in the province of Quebec. All these resources-the energy

resources, the iron and the water-are available. We have the basic resources. Transport is not a serious problem.
I should like once again to refer to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) and to what he said in the speech he made in Calgary. These are his words:
Canada must broaden and diversify its economy and the only way we can do that is make use of all our resources.
In the Atlantic area we have available resources that are not being utilized to the full. Even regardless of new resources and new enterprises, what about the enterprises that are now established? I maintain that our government should be able to do a great deal that would help the enterprises that are now established.
One of the first things I would advocate would be that the government encourage the people of the Atlantic area to have more purchasing power. One of the ways in which they might be able to do this is to encourage the establishment of unions, especially for those who work on the sea, the fishermen, and those who work in the woods of Newfoundland. Another thing which our government might do is to encourage Canadian ownership of the enterprises and industrial resources of the Atlantic area. This statement applies especially with regard to ownership of the coal mines and ownership of the enterprises having to do with the woods in that area. The Prime Minister assured Canadians that he would encourage the co-operative movement. Very little, if anything, has been done in this regard on the part of the government of the day. I believe that the government of Canada ought to encourage the activities of the Atlantic provinces economic council. Our government ought to consider the interests of the Atlantic area when amending tariffs and when considering freight rates.
Over the lunch hour I looked at what the Minister of Transport had to say last week. He said that the alterations to the Vacation-land would cost $2 million. Even that amount in addition to the purchase price of $3 million would mean a total cost of $5 million. For the sum of $5 million the people of that island might have improvement almost immediately rather than having to wait for years hence for the possible expenditure, after many elections, of $100 million or more on a causeway. The province of Newfoundland needs regular railroads and it needs highways. The province of New Brunswick needs highways. All of those people need vast expenditures on behalf of health and educational services.
Promises to Atlantic Provinces
The Prime Minister won 25 of 33 ridings in the Atlantic provinces. He won them on the basis of his assurance that a new deal was on the way. The present practice of delay and procrastination, of only a little bit now and then, only enough to keep them at bay for the time being and of assuring them of a little bit after another election, is hardly good enough. This is a time for greatness. Four out of the ten provinces are involved. In this area Canada was begun. The potentialities are great for the building of Canadian unity and for real national development. Unless action is taken we may see a demagogue arising in the years ahead. We have had in the past some indication that the area is not averse to demagogues. We may have arising a demagogue who may make such an appeal to the electorate there that we may end up by being four Canadas rather than one. I am sure that none of us wants that to happen.

Mr. Speaker, this is the time which is usually taken up by hon. members stating grievances. At the outset I should say that Yukoners are somewhat hardened to the apparent lack of awareness, shall I say, of the Yukon on the part of a great many Canadians in all parts of the country. There exists a general unawareness of the very existence of the Yukon. This is a situation that apparently obtains across Canada. As one travels across the country one sees the coats of arms of various provinces displayed in air line terminals and other public buildings but the coat of arms of the Yukon is not in evidence. This is also true of Canada House in New York.
The very fact that the building is called Canada House suggests to me and other Yukoners that it should be representative of all of Canada and yet we find there an absence of the coats of arms of the Yukon and

of the Northwest Territories. My concern this evening is not with this isolated instance. This is but one of a great many instances one could cite illustrating what I have referred to as a lack of awareness of the existence of the Yukon or, if you will, an absence of a tendency to include the Yukon in this sort of thing.
My observation this evening is much more serious and concerns the representation of all parts of Canada in the memorial chamber in this building. Before I pursue this thought any further I should say that upon my discussing the absence of the coats of arms of the Yukon and Northwest Territories in the main rotunda of this building last year with the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Hamilton) action was taken between the last session and this and we now see these two coats of arms carved and evident in the rotunda of the building. In the memorial chamber, however, their absence is still felt.
On Armistice day in 1928 the then prime minister opened the memorial chamber with these words:
In the name of the people of Canada in proud and grateful remembrance of 60,000 of her sons and daughters whose lives were given in the cause of freedom, I unlock the doors of this memorial chamber, and declare it henceforth open to the public.
Here upon its walls is inscribed the record of their deeds, and upon its altar will rest the book of remembrance containing their names. This then is the very heart of Canada wherein their memory will be cherished forever.
The point I wish to make is that among the 60,000 dead of the first world war there were a goodly number of Yukon citizens who lost their lives. In this regard I might just mention that in November of 1914, Mr. J. W. Boyle of Dawson City, Yukon, later Lieutenant Colonel Boyle, on his own initiative raised the Boyle mounted machine gun detachment. It consisted of some 50 of all ranks. Boyle clothed these men in frontier-men's uniform and despatched them to Vancouver, where they were billeted at his expense. Included in that group was Hon. George Black who once occupied the chair in this house. The detachment was attached first to the 29th battalion and then to the 2nd Canadian Mounted Rifles Regiment. In June, 1915, the Yukon detachment, as it was then called, accompanied the latter unit to England, without horses or guns and was stationed in the Shorncliffe area. On the same ship bearing the detachment to England and I believe later to France was another former member of this house, the late Mrs. George Black. Some of the personnel went to France as reinforcements for the 2nd Canadian Mounted Rifles-converted from 66968-9-282

Coats of Arms in Memorial Chamber cavalry to an infantry battalion of the 3rd division-and other units in the field.
On June 14, 1916, now 33 strong, the detachment was renamed Yukon motor machine gun battery and brought up to an authorized strength of 4 officers and 55 men. Captain H. R. Meurling, an instructor at the Canadian machine gun school, assumed command. The battery went to Bramshott early in July, to join the 4th division as divisional troops. Motor cars and motorcycles were received later in July and six Vickers machine guns early in August. The unit crossed the channel on August 12, 1916, and became E battery of the 1st Canadian motor machine gun brigade.
The battery served at the Somme, October-November, 1916; Vimy Ridge, April, 1917; Hill 70, August, 1917 and Passchendaele, October-November, 1917. On March 22, 1918, the second day of the great German offensive, the motor machine gun brigade was ordered to the Somme in support of the British fifth army. It left the following day, and for twelve days harassed and hindered the enemy's advance.
On May 23 Captain Meurling was promoted and given command of another MG battery. On June 8, E battery, till then still known unofficially by its Yukon title, was broken up and absorbed into the 2nd Canadian motor machine gun brigade. Its commander at that time was Captain F. W. Thompson. The Yukon battery earned a number of decorations in the field, although details regarding decorations received and casualties suffered are not readily available.
In the memorial chamber the altar rests upon black marble steps which were the gift of Great Britain. Above it and around the steps of the altar are the Royal arms, the arms of Canada and the coats of arms of the provinces. The coats of arms of the Yukon and Northwest Territories are not included among the coats of arms of the provinces nor are they included in the golden book of remembrance embossed within which are the names and ranks of all casualties suffered across Canada during the first war. I feel that all hon. members of this house will agree with me, after having heard a brief history of the part that Yukon volunteers played in the last war, that she has earned her right to be included in the memorial chamber.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this government cure the omissions of the past by investigating the circumstances which I described this evening with a view to finding some way of carving the Yukon coat of arms on the altar of the memorial chamber. If the circumstances equally apply to the part

Grain Shipments through Seaway played by the Northwest Territories in the first war, then I would suggest that the coat of arms of the Northwest Territories also be included. There is even a strong argument for its inclusion under any circumstances.

I think, Mr. Speaker, that those in charge of those matters, at a time when we are so concerned about traditions of this kind, should get the utmost attention from the government in the matter not only of our national crest but, as the hon. member has indicated, in the matter of the Memorial Chamber, and recognition in the building and in other places.

Mr. Speaker, the grievance I should like to raise this evening has to do with the grain producers of western Canada. Before launching into that. Mr. Speaker, I hope I may be allowed merely to say that had I not been dealing with this general subject I would have been very

happy at this time to add the support of this group to the very pertinent remarks of the hon. member for the Yukon.
The issue that I wish to raise has to do with the very low delivery quotas prevailing at the present time in western Canada. It has to do with the very drastic falling off of lakehead shipments of grain through the seaway and the general adverse results as far as western grain producers are concerned. I have raised this matter a number of times this session on the orders of the day and I have received from the ministers evasive replies, misinformation and apparently a complete unawareness of the very adverse conditions prevailing at a great many marketing points. There are many reasons, perhaps, or a number of reasons why this situation is as bad as it is, but certainly one of the most important reasons is the fact that since the opening of navigation, lakehead shipments have been much lower this year than a year ago. I hold in my hand a Canadian Press report which appeared on June 1, and which reads in part as follows:
Fort William. Only 55 million bushels of grain have been shipped from the lakehead during the 1959 navigation season compared with 104 million bushels in the corresponding period of 1958.
I had hoped when I raised this grievance, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) would be in his seat. In his absence, I sent a note over to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees). In fairness to the Minister of Transport I must say that he replied to me that he had a previous engagement which would make it impossible for him to remain in the chamber.

On a point of order, the
minister is in the building, but perhaps not in his seat.

That has nothing to do with his note. Surely, the minister will acknowledge that what I said was completely accurate. I do not have to produce the note, surely.
The very drastic drop in shipments of grain through the lakehead is apparently brought about by the inability of the St. Lawrence seaway to handle grain shipments, along with other shipments, in the same volume this year as last year. Since the seaway opened there has been one report after another of congestion, of inability to move ships quickly through the canal, and generally of a situation of very great inefficiency. Because of this congestion, because of a lack of priority for Canadian basic products, the seaway has been unable to provide facilities for the shipment of large quantities of grain this year as compared with last year.

There was an editorial in the Montreal Gazette on June 1 dealing with the congestion of the Welland canal, and it had this to say:
Last year it was possible for Canadian ships to pass through the Welland canal in nine hours. This year it is taking up to 58 hours. Not only are the costs of these delays being added to what Canadians must pay, but the level of tolls, imposed for the opening of the waterway, is yet another addition to the cost structure.
It goes on to say:
Unless Canadian shipping is given reasonable priority in the Welland locks, the Canadian economy may be seriously injured by the St. Lawrence waterway instead of being aided by it, and this surely, after all that has been said about the waterway, would be the height of irony.
Because of the inability of grain shipments to be taken through the seaway in substantial quantities I suggest that now is the time for the government to consider this problem and to act. 1 was pleased this afternoon to hear that the Minister of Transport has made a request to the United States that its flotilla of ships that are to appear in the seaway should go through the canal locks at the rate of only two a day. I would go even further. I would say that if the appearance of those ships in the seaway is to adversely affect the shipment of Canadian products through the seaway, as would appear from reports in today's newspapers, reported by people who are authorities on the seaway, then it would be far better if United States ships stayed at home and if grain, iron ore and other Canadian products went through the seaway. Authorities are telling us that if they all go through at the same time it would make such a tie-up and such a mess that it will take a period of three weeks to unravel the conditions that are brought about by the appearance of so many ships.
These are military ships.

Yes, they are military ships, it does not matter what ships they are; they are going to block the canal.
I raised this question on May 21, Mr. Speaker. I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce to comment on the very drastic drop at that time from 72 million bushels being shipped through the seaway a year ago to 33 million bushels this year, and the minister replied as follows, as reported at page 3870 of Hansard:
I did not require notice of this question from the hon. member. The 47 Conservative members from the prairie provinces are also interested in this matter and have been talking to me about it in the interval. We are not dependent upon one lone figure to draw our attention to these important facts in Canada.
Then he goes on with a real clincher.
I make no comment with regard to the shipping and the seaway facilities; that is not my province.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce, under whose department comes the sale, delivery and export of grain, says "I make no comment" as a result of a drop of 50 per cent in the shipment of grain through the seaway. I raised this question again on June 1. I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce the following question, as found at page 4196 of Hansard:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, arising out of the very drastic reduction in shipments of grain from the lakehead. Can the minister explain why shipments from the lakehead since the opening of navigation have dropped from 86 million bushels last year to only 42 million bushels this year, and whether anything is being done to speed up shipments through the St. Lawrence seaway?
The minister replied that farm deliveries were good and that quotas were satisfactory. He did everything but deal with the question I raised. Then I tried a supplementary question.
What date was this?

June 1, page 4197 of Hansard. I asked the minister this supplementary question:
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to know whether there might be some improvement in this very drastic reduction in shipments out of the lakehead, and I am asking the minister whether he can make any statement on that point. I would like him to comment as to why almost consistently since the opening of navigation Canadian exports are down this year as compared with a year ago.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce replied:
Mr, Speaker, that last statement is quite incorrect. Canadian exports are holding up extraordinarily well.
Then I went on to say:
I am not talking about the year in question; I am talking about recent weeks since the opening of navigation. The graph put out by the minister's own department shows a very substantial reduction. I can send it across to the minister.
I tried the same question the next day and I had figures to substantiate the statement I had made before, namely that Canadian exports had dropped. I asked the minister to explain why Canadian exports from April 22 to May 20 this year were just 15.9 million bushels compared with 25.1 million bushels in the same period last year. After some crossfire the minister replied as follows:
It may well be that exports of wheat during the month of April have been slightly lower than a year ago-
He did not know that the day before but on June 2 he admitted they were down. They were down in April following the opening of navigation and they have been down in May of this year. I have in my hand the latest figures taken from the Canadian wheat board

Grain Shipments through Seaway statistical summary and the board of grain commissioners weekly report. Overseas clearances of wheat from April 11 to May 27 this year amounted to 25.3 million bushels and in the same period last year exports amounted to 35.9 million bushels.
I am glad that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) is in his seat, I ask him if this very substantial drop in exports is not a serious matter, if it is not so important that the government should reply and explain why this very drastic drop in exports of Canadian wheat has taken place since the opening of navigation. When I put the question to the minister that the falling off of shipments from the lakehead might be having an adverse effect on Canadian exports he said no. He said that we had sufficient grain on hand at seaway ports and that even though the St. Lawrence seaway has been unable to handle the volume of grain that was handled a year ago there is enough at the seaway ports to take care of all exports.
I would suggest that that puts the matter in an even more serious perspective in that it shows that there has been no loss of export markets because grain was not available and yet, as I have said, from April 22 to May 27 there has been a drop in exports of wheat from 35.9 million bushels in the same period a year ago to 25.3 million bushels this year. These figures show that since the opening of navigation exports of Canadian wheat are not running anywhere nearly as high as they were a year ago and the situation in the present crop year, which has so far not been as bright as last year, is being made even worse in relation to the export sales of the other major exporting countries.
I have in my hand a Canadian Press article which appeared in the Globe and Mail of June 8 and is based on a dominion bureau of statistics report. It reads in part as follows:
Canadian wheat and flour exports in the August-March period dropped to 188,100,000 bushels from
197.600.000	a year earlier despite a 9 per cent gain in the total market of the big four wheat shippers, the United States, Canada, Argentina and Australia.
From August to March of this year Canadian wheat exports were down 9.5 million bushels or 5 per cent from a year ago. In the same period United States exports were
298.200.000	bushels, up from 255,500,000 bushels a year ago, or an increase for the United States of 43 million bushels or 17 per cent. Argentina's exports were up to 62 million bushels this year from 48,500,000 a year ago, an increase of 13.5 million bushels or 28 per cent. Australia's exports were also up to 50,400,000 bushels this year compared

with 46,400,000 bushels last year, an increase of 4 million bushels or 9 per cent.
In the wheat picture in the world today Canada's exports are down while exports by the United States, Argentina and Australia have increased substantially. When we ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce why Canadian exports are down he first of all denies it. Later he says that the reduction in the shipment of grain through the seaway has not adversely affected Canadian exports. So I ask, why has there been such a substantial falling off in Canadian exports since the opening of navigation compared with a year ago? If the grain does not go through the lakehead and through the seaway, if the grain pipe line, as it is called in popular terms, is plugged at Fort William and Port Arthur, this can only mean a falling off of deliveries of wheat and other grains by Canadian wheat producers.
For the period from April 22 to May 27 I find that a year ago farmers delivered 40.7 million bushels of wheat and that in the same period this year there has been a decrease in deliveries of more than 13 million bushels to just 27.3 million bushels. Deliveries from the farms are falling off as one would expect with such a drastic reduction in shipments of wheat and other grains through the lake-head. In the period April 22 to May 27 total deliveries of all grains from farms amounted to 49.4 million bushels a year ago and this year the figure is just 35.8 million bushels, a reduction of approximately 20 per cent this year compared with last year.
Mr. Speaker, the end of the crop year is not far away. The end of the crop year is July 31. Between now and July 31 the Canadian wheat board and the Canadian grain trade have approximately seven weeks in which to provide relative equality of treatment for the grain producers in the prairie provinces. Over the years I have been a strong advocate of a quota system but of a quota system that is equalized during the crop year. No one can expect that quotas can be equalized every day. Everyone who knows anything about the grain business nows that there are certain reasons why grain from time to time is taken from certain delivery points and not from certain other delivery points. But surely it should be the objective of any administration as well as of everyone who is attached to the grain trade in Canada to see to it that in so far as it may be possible provision is made for equal delivery quotas for all producers by the end of the crop year.
What is the situation now? The latest weekly report from the Canadian wheat board which came to my office today shows

that of the three prairie provinces, Alberta is in by far the best situation. For regular quotas there were six points on a four-bushel quota; 135 points on a five-bushel quota; 170 points on a six-bushel quota and 174 points on a seven-bushel quota.	In the
province of Alberta 70 per cent of all regular delivery quotas were in excess of four bushels per acre, that is of the regular delivery quotas.
In the province of Saskatchewan, as to regular delivery quotas, there were 69 points on a three-bushel quota; 551 points on a four-bushel quota; 318 points on a five-bushel quota; 82 points on a six-bushel quota and 36 points on a seven-bushel quota.	Unlike
Alberta which has 70 per cent of its points on quotas in excess of five bushels per acre, Saskatchewan has just 11 per cent of the marketing points on this kind of quota in excess of five bushels per acre.
In Manitoba the situation is as bad and perhaps even worse. In Manitoba there are 88 points on a three-bushel quota; 219 points on a four-bushel quota; 50 points on a five-bushel quota; 12 points on a six-bushel quota and 3 points on a seven-bushel quota. In the provnce of Manitoba only some 4 per cent of the marketing points are on a quota in excess of five bushels per acre. This is a tremendous discrepancy. This means that for the great majority of the areas of western Canada, at those points most producers face a marketing quota of three bushels, four bushels or five bushels per acre. Yet at the same time there is a substantial number of points on a six-bushel and a seven-bushel quota. I am hoping that an extraordinary effort will now be made within the next few weeks to bring up the points with a low quota so that there can be greater equality of treatment in western Canada.
I have in my hand a number of maps and charts showing the quota situation prevailing in Saskatchewan on June 1. On looking at these charts one finds that marketing points for the special quota for tough and damp grain, are concentrated in northeast Saskatchewan. A number of times on the orders of the day I asked the government to give special consideration to providing what I termed emergency quotas for the delivery of tough and damp grain. This action apparently has now been taken. I would be interested in finding out when it was taken.
I am given certain information that would suggest to me that it is something that has taken place only in recent weeks. In any event I think it has been a good action, namely that farmers who have tough and damp grain should be given an opportunity of marketing as large quantities as possible before the grain deteriorates and is lost.

However, I also have in my hand a chart of the seven-bushel quotas per specified acre. These quotas are not emergency quotas dealing with tough and damp grain; they are regular quotas to take in regular grades of wheat as the farmers deliver it. There is still a substantial concentration of these marketing quotas in northeastern Saskatchewan. The quotas prevail in an area which extends northeast from Saskatoon and southeast from Prince Albert. With the exception of a very few-and there are a few-other points on a seven-bushel quota, the great majority of the points on this quota are concentrated in that area. The six-bushel quota is somewhat more evenly divided but it is still more prevalent in the northeastern and now in the northwestern part of Saskatchewan. The five-bushel quota and the four-bushel quota are scattered about the province but the four-bushel quota is concentrated to a large extent in the southern part of the province of Saskatchewan.
I might say, Mr. Speaker, if I have not already made it clear, that these maps have to do with Saskatchewan only. The quotas in southern and southeastern Saskatchewan are extremely low and I would suggest that they constitute at this time an emergency situation. In the Saskatchewan wheat pool district 3A the latest quotas are as follows: 14 points are on a three-bushel quota; 75 points are on a four-bushel quota and only 13 of the points in that area are on quotas in excess of five bushels. This means that farmers in this area as well as other areas of Manitoba, in other areas of Saskatchewan and perhaps even in some areas of Alberta have not had an equal opportunity, or anything approaching an equal opportunity, to deliver grain at this time.
This situation has been brought about certainly in some substantial degree by the great failure of the St. Lawrence seaway facilities and failure of people in the grain business to pay attention to the need for putting shipments of grain out of the lake-head through the seaway. The Minister of Trade and Commerce says he has no responsibility. If he wants to abrogate his responsibility, if he wants to give it to some other minister, I suggest that the responsibility after all lies with the government. I suggest it is the responsibility of the government to take extraordinary measures to remove the bottlenecks in the seaway and to make certain that Canadian shipments of grain from now to the end of the crop year are given absolute priority of movement through the seaway. It will be too late if the bottleneck has been removed after July 31. Some of the farmers will find they have ended the crop year without an opportunity to deliver

Grain Shipments through Seaway a fair quota of grain and they will be crippled economically because the government has failed to deal with this situation. There has been a transport controller in the past; perhaps the government needs a transport controller today, but it is certainly necessary for someone in authority to see that grain shipments are moved out of the lakehead to protect Canadian overseas markets and to give grain producers on the prairies between now and the end of July a chance to delivery quotas on a more equitable basis.
I would suggest secondly that the government should take emergency action of whatever kind may be necessary to provide all of the box cars that are necessary at low delivery points to give the farmers at those points an opportunity to deliver grain up to I would say at least a 7-bushel quota.
Third, if the government still denies that this situation is as I have pictured it, then I would say that there should be a thorough inquiry by a committee of this house to ascertain why lakehead clearances have dropped by such a drastic and alarming amount as compared with last year. I say that such a committee should inquire into why Canadian exports since the opening of navigation are down, and should inquire why delivery quotas have discriminated to such an enormous degree against producers in certain widespread areas of western Canada.
As a fourth step that I suggest the government needs to take, and I would suggest is morally bound to take, they should decide and announce in this house their policy on deficiency payments and their reply to the grain producers and the briefs they have presented to the government. When we have asked the government what they are going to do about the submissions made by the farm organizations, we get this pat reply. "The government is giving the submission consideration." The submission was submitted to the government on March 10. It has been giving consideration to this now for three months. How long, Mr. Speaker, must the government give consideration to this important submission before it decides on its policy?
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. For our guidance, would it be possible for the hon. member to tell us how he can relate-my friend is too anxious to get up.
Well, I have the floor.

The hon. member took his seat; will he allow me to put my question? How can the hon. member relate deficiency payments to his grievance that wheat was not moving this year through the lakehead?

How does the hon. member relate these two and bear upon the rule of repetition in the house on deficiency payments?

Now my friend has raised two points of order, and until the house takes a decision on deficiency payments it is in order to raise the question at an appropriate place, and it is relevant to the question under discussion. I shall answer the hon. gentleman, Mr. Speaker, by merely referring to what I said when I opened my remarks. I said that I wished to raise a grievance having to do with the general grain situation on the prairies. Then I went on, after having made those opening remarks, and talked about the drop in shipments through the seaway. I raise this fourth point, Mr. Speaker. Under the general grain situation and the general grievance affecting the grain situation that I have presented tonight I say that it is time this government quit procrastinating and time they quit fooling the prairie grain producers that in fact they are really giving the question of deficiency payments serious consideration.
I asked a supplementary question of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) after the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) had raised this point on May 26. I asked this question as recorded on page 4011 of Hansard of that date:
Can the Prime Minister say whether, following the consideration that is now being given, a decision will be made during the present session of parliament so that if it is necessary to introduce legislation in order to implement the government's decision, that can be done?
To that the Prime Minister replied as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I would not want to answer that question directly, for the reason that it depends on the length of time during which consideration is given to the request.
The Prime Minister left it open for himself and the cabinet to give consideration to this request, and has done so for months to come, certainly for weeks to come, until the session is ended and until it will be impossible for the house to deal with any legislation that might be required if a decision were favourable. Mr. Speaker, in the name of the grain producers of western Canada I ask the government to come to their assistance in these last weeks of the crop year to provide priorities for the movement of grain through the lakehead, to provide whatever box cars are necessary to allow producers at low delivery points the opportunity to deliver at least a 7-bushel or 8-bushel quota as is being provided for other groups. In the meantime I ask, if the government denies the facts which I have presented, for a thorough inquiry by a committee of this

house as to why lakehead clearances are down, as to why exports have fallen, and as to why delivery quotas are discriminating against so many marketing points and against so many producers in western Canada. I ask the government to take emergency action to remove the bottleneck in the shipments of Canadian grain so that Canadian producers may have the opportunity to deliver substantial quantities of grain before the crop season ends.
Finally, I make a plea that the government ends its procrastination to make a decision and informs the house as to what its decision is on deficiency payments, so that if a favourable decision is made, as I trust it will, parliament during this session will have the opportunity to pass whatever estimates or whatever legislation is necessary to implement that decision.
May I ask a question, Mr. Speaker? Is the hon. member now changing his story, and will he not admit that most farmers have enough wheat on their farms to fill an 8-bushel quota?
Mr. Speaker, if a farmer has an 8-bushel quota, it does not mean that he has the grain to deliver the quota. I am merely asking this very simple thing-
Will the hon. member answer my question? Have they enough to fill an 8-bushel quota?
Some have and some have not. Mr. Speaker, there are 235,000 or a few more holders of permit books on the prairies. Some have enough grain-
Will the hon. member give an idea how many they could have?

Mr. Speaker, I do not think this is a very pertinent point. The pertinent point is whether the farmers in the prairie provinces will have the opportunity to deliver an 8-bushel quota. If they have not the grain at home then they cannot take advantage of that opportunity. There are certain quotas and a certain limited number of points in the west today that are on what are called limited quotas, and in the definition of the Canadian wheat board these are quotas which are now in existence at certain marketing points at a figure high enough to take deliveries. I think the Canadian wheat board can give these statistics to my hon. friend, but I will give him the answer. As of May 25, 1959, in Saskatchewan-and I can give the figures for the three prairie provinces-1,056 points were on regular quotas and only 31 points were on a limited quota, namely on quotas at 31 points which, in the opinion of the wheat board, were ample to take
Grain Shipments through Seaway care of the grain which farmers had ready for delivery in those districts. The fact is that many thousands of western wheat producers at this time are crying out for the opportunity to deliver grain, and quotas are being denied to them.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
there are three subjects which, I believe, the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) raised, and I suppose I should be the last one to deal in the house with deficiency payments and the movement of wheat.
However, there is a matter in which I am particularly interested, and that is the first part of the grievance which the hon. member for Assiniboia raised, namely the bottlenecks on the Welland canal and on the seaway resulting in a lack of grain deliveries and leading, also, to difficulty in the movement of grain. The point which the hon. member makes has to do with drastic reductions in grain deliveries out of the lakehead; his point was that Canadian exports have declined since last year. I am not in a position to challenge that statement, nor do I, but what I do say is that if that is the case it is not due to anything that is happening on the Welland canal. The proof of that lies in the fact that up till now, when barely more than two months of the navigation season have gone by, almost twice as much traffic, notwithstanding what is happening, has gone through as in the same period last year.
However, that does not derogate from the fact that the government and the Minister of Transport are not applying the right policies to remedy what is happening, and to that extent I find myself in accord with the hon. member for Assiniboia. We all know that the early delays on the seaway were caused by ice conditions.

If the hon. member intends to speak about matters other than this question of grain deliveries I wonder if he would mind if I replied to that aspect of the debate now, and then we could go on to the other subject.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am sorry, but I have to go out of the house to a meeting, and I am ten minutes late. I think I can dispose of this within the next few minutes, but I do want to bring to the attention of the house the fact that here are reasons for the bottlenecks which have arisen, and that the congestion could, in my opinion, have been averted. I think that if a decision had been taken in the first place to open navigation on a fixed date, and not postpone it twice, there would not have been that congestion of ships at Montreal waiting to enter the seaway, creating a bottleneck which afterwards continued in the Welland canal.

Grain Shipments through Seaway
I made a suggestion during the question period which was turned down without any consideration whatsoever being given to it. That was that the introduction of sector gates at the Thorold locks of the Welland canal such as those which exist in the lower locks would speed up traffic considerably. I have since been informed by competent engineers that this is a fact and that their introduction would help tremendously in the movement of ships.
I think, in all fairness to the Minister of Transport, that it is still too early to come to a decision on the present position of traffic on the seaway. I think that the seaway must be given a trial period, and this trial period would certainly be not less than the length of the navigation season and perhaps more. One cannot in two or three months make a decision as to what should be done. But there is one thing which I hope will be considered by the minister. I asked him this question and he hedged in his reply: whether or not the engineers of the special projects branch of the seaway authority should not now be giving careful consideration to the duplication of certain of the Thorold locks on the Welland canal. While the engineers are doing that, it might be possible to arrive at a suggestion, with other studies-one or two of which I am going to make-as to whether or not traffic conditions can be substantially improved.
I think, too, that there is a very serious lack of co-ordination between three bodies in the Department of Transport-the national harbours board, the seaway authority and the St. Lawrence ship channel authority. Those three bodies, I am sorry to say, did not work in co-operation during the early part of the navigation season, and it is because of this lack of co-operation that, in my opinion, there has been the first delays which have since been continued.
I am glad that the Minister of Transport announced today that the flotilla or convoy of United States ships will, perhaps, not be introduced into the seaway. My suggestion is that it should be allowed to remain at Montreal and that it be not allowed to go into the seaway at all, because if there is congestion now, as reports in the press indicate, and as even the minister's statements -some of which are quite contradictory- indicate, there is certainly no reason in the world to clutter up the canal more than is the case at the present time. All this traffic, however, goes to show that the seaway is certainly going to be a success, as has been suggested in the house, at this time of the year so early in the period of navigation.

Then there is the really important question of whether or not there should be discrimination against Canadian ships. I raised the question on the orders of the day, and was told, in reply, that there was a system of priorities in existence which staggered a foreign ship and a Canadian ship in so far as bulk cargoes were concerned and it was felt that there should be no change in the procedure in the meantime because, I think the minister said, there were four ships waiting to enter the canal at Port Weller and about five waiting to enter the canal at Port Col-borne on the downward movement or vice versa. That is a matter for which the government is responsible. I remember quite well what the statements were in so far as discrimination was concerned when the matter was discussed many years ago, but whether or not in view of what is happening there should be a system of priorities affecting Canadian traffic is a matter for the government to determine. But I say that the government should determine that as soon as possible having regard to the reports which have been made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) from time to time.
I think that the minister should at the first opportunity-that is Wednesday when his estimates are being discussed in this house- make a statement on this subject. He is in possession of the facts; he has the reports from his engineers and he is familiar with the statistics which have been compiled concerning the movement of ships. I think he owes it to the house and to the country to make a complete statement on the present position-not partial statements such as we have heard from time to time in the question and answer period. That is not sufficient, and I think that until such a full statement is made it will not be possible for us to make up our minds about the seriousness of these delays on the canal and the confusion which has been reported. I therefore invite the minister to make this statement at the earliest possible moment.

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to go into transportation matters at all in my discussion this evening. However, I should like to make a few comments on the speech made by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue). The hon. member as usual attempted to paint a picture of gloom and anticipated despair on the western prairie as a result of the inability of farmers to market their grain. Nothing could be further from the true facts than the type of picture he attempted to leave in the minds of hon. members in this regard.
You cannot get away from the facts and statistics.

The hon. member repeated time after time with somewhat monotonous regularity the statement that Canadian exports are down this year. At one point he said that Canadian exports of wheat are drastically down this year. Naturally he implied all of the evil results that would flow from our exports being drastically down.
What is the true situation in this regard? The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) put the figures on the record only a few days ago, on June 1, when he stated that up to the end of March of this year exports of wheat and flour were just under 9 million bushels below the figure for the same period last year. That is the drastic decline to which the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) referred. Last year exports of wheat from this country amounted to 316 million bushels-

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The minister will recall that in my remarks I was referring to the drastic reduction in exports since the opening of navigation. In order to be completely fair
1	took the exports from the beginning of the first full week following the opening of navigation.
That is not a point of order. That is an argument.

The hon. member is not
advancing a point of order but merely engaging in counter argument. The hon. member repeated time after time that our exports of wheat are drastically down.
Since the opening of navigation they are drastically down.

The hon. gentleman
attempted to paint a picture of gloom and despair as far as the western farmer is concerned. The true picture as I said is depicted by the information placed on the record by the Minister of Trade and Commerce on June
2	as reported at page 4242 of Hansard. Our exports are down just 9 million bushels below a year ago. Down 9 million bushels from what? From 316 million bushels which we exported in the last crop year as compared with 267 or 268 million bushels exported in the previous crop year. The hon. member neglected entirely to point out the fact that in the first year this government was in office we managed to secure a marked increase in the exports of wheat from Canada.

Now you are falling behind again. Exports are down.

Three hundred and sixteen million bushels were exported in the last crop year as compared with 267 or 268 million in the previous crop year.
You are falling behind once more. Exports are declining.

The hon. gentleman is now talking about a drop of 9 million bushels from the figure I mentioned up to date. We have not yet reached the end of the crop year. The hon. gentleman described it as a drastic decline which is a typical example of the exaggerated language in which the hon. member unfortunately engages.
As a matter of fact, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the chairman of the wheat board, various members of the wheat board, and various members of the government including myself have stated on several occasions during the past months that we expected our exports of wheat this year to reach at least 300 million bushels. We still expect our exports to reach that figure. The amount we have exported thus far gives every indication that this target will be reached. If we do reach exports of 300 million bushels then all the other complaints the hon. member has been making about quotas will disappear.
Not at all.

This will mean that practically all the farmers in western Canada will have been able to deliver all of the wheat they wanted to deliver to the elevators. When you subtract the amount they want to retain for seed and so on there will be few farmers in western Canada who will have any wheat that they have been unable to deliver.
We will see on July 31.

speechtext: Order.

The hon. member went on to say that Canadian exports are down whereas Argentine and Australian exports are up. What he neglected to say was that Australia had a crop failure last year and actually imported wheat from Canada. As proof that Canada is not doing well the hon. member pointed out that Australian exports are up. Naturally they would be up if Australia had no crop failure this year as was the case last year. With typical lack of logic the hon. member attempted to take an extraordinary year as far as Australia is concerned to prove his point that Canada is not doing very well in wheat exports. We know that Australia last year actually imported wheat from Canada. That is an indication of what a completely unfair, biased

Grain Shipments through Seaway argument the hon. gentleman advanced and illustrates the incorrect impression he attempted to convey.
The hon. gentleman went on to exclaim that there were very low delivery quotas. Rather than being low, delivery quotas are the best they have been for a number of years. They are better than they have been for a number of years in the past. I do not have on hand the exact period this would cover but they are better than they have been for a considerable length of time. The hon. member read off a long list of delivery quotas but neglected to refer to what the Minister of Trade and Commerce told him as reported at page 4197 of Hansard of June 2 when the minister said:
If he has any further worry with regard to the quota distribution in the prairie provinces, may I assure him that this year at this time there are 264 stations on a 7-bushel quota per specified acre; last year there were none. This year there are 308 stations on a 6-bushel quota per specified acre; last year there were 341. Generally the picture is much better than it was a year ago.
The hon. member having been told this and knowing it of his own knowledge still rose in his place and said that delivery quotas are low and that a serious situation exists in western Canada because farmers cannot deliver their grain.
I have in my hand the Regina Leader-Post of Friday, June 5, 1959 which contains an article entitled, "Board Not Concerned by Small Wheat Export" which is a statement of the wheat board.
I thought there was a big wheat export; you said there was.

The hon. gentleman should let me make my speech. I did not interrupt him. The article states in part:
The Canadian wheat board Thursday announced new increases in grain delivery quotas at provincial points.
The following increases are effective immediately-
That is, effective on Friday. The article then lists 24 points that are to be put on a 4-bushel quota, 50 points that are to be put on a 5-bushel quota, 19 points that are to be put on a 6-bushel quota and 16 points that are to be put on a 7-bushel quota. These are all Saskatchewan points. The article then lists increases that are to be effective on Monday; in other words, today. A further 34 points are to be put on a 4-bushel quota, a further 96 points are to be put on a 5-bushel quota, a further 28 points are to be put on a 6-bushel quota, a further 5 points are to be put on a 7-bushel quota and a further 11 points are to be put on an 8-bushel quota.
In other words, due to the fact that we have been exporting grain at a very satis-

factory rate this year the delivery quotas are rapidly going up in Saskatchewan and Manitoba. They were already somewhat higher in Alberta as the hon. member said. I have no doubt that the hon. gentleman, if he read this newspaper article-
No, I did not.
Certainly he should not be making speeches such as he made in the house when delivery quotas on Friday last and today were considerably increased in the very province about which he was complaining.
The picture I painted was accurate.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I must remind the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) that he is not entitled to speak from his seat when another hon. member has the floor. It would be appreciated if he did not constantly interrupt the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness). If the hon. member for Assiniboia wants the floor he may have it at some other time.

Mr. Speaker, I do not mind the hon. member interrupting because I know this hurts a little and therefore I expect to hear him squeal to a certain extent.
Having disposed of this complaint raised by the hon. member for Assiniboia that very low delivery quotas obtained this year and having indicated that exactly the reverse is the true situation I should like to turn to the remarks the hon. gentleman made about low shipments from lakehead ports. Just the reverse is the case. I should like to say something about what he had to say about low shipments from lakehead ports. I should like to ask him, or any other hon. member here, if any exports have been lost as a result of the lower shipments from lakehead ports this year. There is not an hon. member in this house who can say that any has been lost.
Why then are they down?

In this same paper is a statement from the wheat board in which they state:
A spokesman of the Canadian wheat board said there is no problem,-
He is talking about small shipments from the head of the lakes this year. I continue:
-there is no problem, as plenty of wheat is in store at eastern elevators right now.
In other words, we have not lost the sale of a single bushel of grain because the shipments on the lakes are lower this year than they were last year. The hon. member was building up a great big strawman, and then

trying to make a big fellow of himself by punching holes in it, by talking about those low grain shipments from the head of the lakes this year. This has not lost us a bushel of exports, not one, and therefore, this was all shadow-boxing by the hon. member for Assiniboia.
Then, he made an attack on the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) in connection with his saying that he had no comment to make on the transportation difficulties on the great lakes. After reading what the Minister of Trade and Commerce had to say, which was as follows:
I make no comment with regard to the shipping and the seaway facilities-
He made a great point out of the fact that the Minister of Trade and Commerce takes no interest in this; he apparently does not care about the seaway shipments, and so forth and so on, and this was a terrible dereliction of duty on the part of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, but he completely neglected to read what the Minister of Trade and Commerce said after that, which was as follows:
The situation with regard to export trade is being maintained. The fact that the shipment of grain from the lakehead is not as great as it was last year has no effect on our export market at the present time, because there is sufficient grain in position further east to handle these exports. Our exports of wheat are continuing at a good figure. We still expect to reach the quota that we set earlier in the year.
This is on page 3870 of Hansard of May 21. The quota that we set earlier in the year was 300 million bushels, which I mentioned a little while ago. If we reach the 300 million bushels, which I feel quite confident we will, which the members of the wheat board feel quite confident we will, then the number of farmers who will have been unable to deliver the grain they wanted to deliver will be very, very small indeed. As a matter of fact, Mr. Wesson, the head of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, when he was down here on his last trip about 10 days ago, I guess, in connection with deficiency payments, made that very statement to us, that in his opinion the four and five bushel quotas which existed at most points would be more than sufficient to take the grain that the great majority of farmers in western Canada wanted to deliver, let alone going to six, seven and eight bushels quotas which the hon. member was talking about. I would suggest he should get some better information from Mr. Wesson and some of the other people who know something about the grain business and the grain situation in western Canada than the type of information 66968-9-283J
Dominion-Provincial Relations with which he has been attempting to give a completely inaccurate picture to the house this evening.
May I ask a question? Will the minister assure the house that all marketing points at July 31 will have at least a seven bushel quota?
The hon. member knows to begin with that this is not my department, and I am not in a position to give any such assurance to the house, as a result of that.

That is the answer to your own

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON JUDGMENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT ON PROPERTY VALUATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether, now that he has had an opportunity of reading the judgment of the exchequer court concerning the expropriation of land for Malton airport, he has any further statement to make on this matter at the present time.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minisier):
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON JUDGMENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT ON PROPERTY VALUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday the Leader of the Opposition asked this question:
I should like to direct to the Prime Minister a question based on reports of a judgment rendered yesterday by the exchequer court with regard to property valuation at Malton airport. Is it the intention of the Prime Minister to make a statement concerning the matter covered by this judgment, in which the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) and the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Pallett) are mentioned?
In the course of my reply I said, amongst other things:
However, I think I should say at this time that in so far as any reference to any hon. member in this house is concerned, and in particular to the hon. member for Peel, the integrity and honesty of purpose of that hon. member leaves no question in my mind.
I wish to thank the Leader of the Opposition for the support he gave me in this regard when he said:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask a supplementary question. In view of statements made in the judgment- and I am not quarrelling in any way with what the Prime Minister has said-has the Prime Minister considered referring this matter to the appropriate standing committee of the house so that it may be given the fullest and most impartial examination?
I repeat that I very much appreciated the attitude taken by the Leader of the Opposition in entirely supporting me when I said that the honesty and integrity of the hon. member left no question in my mind.
In conformity with the answer I gave, I have read carefully the judgment of the exchequer court and I have also had an opportunity of discussing the matter fully with the Minister of Transport and the hon. member for Peel. On the basis of those discussions and studies the opinion I expressed on Friday is fully confirmed. There is nothing which brings into question the integrity and honesty of the hon. member for Peel, and in so far as the minister is concerned there is, of course, no reference whatsoever throughout the entire judgment which in any way to the slightest degree suggests any impropriety.
I feel I should give some particulars regarding the suggestion that this matter might be referred to a committee. According to the judgment, which I have before me, the matters in question having to do with the valuation of land in the Malton area had their origin in the expropriation proceedings of 1954. During the period from 1954 until June 10, 1957, the hon. member for Peel acted in the capacity of solicitor with regard to this matter for some 14 or 15 veterans in that area who felt that justice was not being done to them in the offers made by the department in respect of the land expropriated.
From June, 1957-and I want to underline this-following the change of government the hon. member for Peel thereafter ceased to have any connection with the legal end, disassociating himself from that position. His endeavours were to secure what he believed to be justice for these particular constituents and veterans. It was not until January, 1959, of course, that the hon. member became chief government whip.
I carefully considered the position on the basis of an examination of that judgment and also in the light of past authorities in

Inquiries oj the Ministry respect of the submission to a committee of matters such as these concerning the privileges of any hon. member of parliament, and I found no case in which any such submission to a committee was ever provided for except where it had been alleged that there was on the part of an hon. member improper conduct resulting in his personal gain. Of that there is not one scintilla of evidence in the judgment or elsewhere as far as the hon. member for Peel is concerned.
I think I should refer to the authorities so the record will be complete in this regard. I say, first, that on the basis of the experience of the past and of the traditions of this house, all the cases referred to the standing committee on privileges and elections since 1867 had to do with alleged improper conduct whereby a member allegedly had used his public position in order to further his private interest. Those cases go back to 1877. In 1877 there was the case of a newspaper owned by Hon. T. W. Anglin, M.P. which became a party to a contract with the Post Office Department concerning the insertion of advertisements relating to the public service. However, parliament having been prorogued no action was taken by the house.
In 1890 J. C. Rykert, M.P., was charged and found guilty of having used his influence to get for one John Adams a grant of certain timber limits. This was brought before the committee and Rykert resigned his seat, having been found guilty.
In 1891 charges were brought against Hon. Thomas McGreevy, member of parliament and member of the Quebec harbours commission in connection with tenders and contracts. The committee found a conspiracy between the contractors and the member in question. A contracting firm had taken the member's brother as partner and given him an interest in the firm in order to obtain a contract. McGreevy resigned his seat.
There was the case in 1915 in which A. deW. Foster, M.P., was found by the public accounts committee to have acted as a purchasing agent for the government in the purchase of certain requirements for the army. That committee reported to the house, recommending thorough investigation and action by the Department of Justice. Before such action was taken, A. deW. Foster resigned his seat. There were four other cases of a similar nature in which the action taken resulted in the charges against the member being rejected.
That in general summarizes the situation under which the rights of parliament are subject to that jealous scrutiny which at all times must be maintained. In every case

there was moral wrongdoing or the achievement of personal gain. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, under those circumstances and reinforced by the objective attitude taken by the Leader of the Opposition when he confirmed me in the general statement I made during the course of my remarks on Friday, there is nothing to be placed before any committee.

It is quite true, as the Prime Minister has said, that I stated in the house on Friday that I had no quarrel with what the Prime Minister said on that occasion. Of course I would have no occasion either to quarrel with or support any statement the Prime Minister made on that occasion, because it was a preliminary statement pending the examination which at that time he promised to make.
Naturally I am glad to confirm what I said on that preliminary occasion. We on this side will now study the Prime Minister's very important statement today. If that statement seems to require further discussion in the house no doubt there will be an opportunity later to refer to it.
I should like to ask the Prime Minister whether he does not agree from a study of the judgment-and I had not an opportunity of making that study last Friday-that there are contradictions between statements in this judgment about a member of parliament and statements made outside the house on the same matter by the same hon. member, contradictions which in fairness to all concerned should be cleared up?

subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON JUDGMENT OF EXCHEQUER COURT ON PROPERTY VALUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know of no contradictions such as are suggested by the Leader of the Opposition. I may say a committee is not set up for the purpose of resolving contradictions. The circumstances under which a committee is set up are very clearly shown to be based upon a charge or charges made by a member of this house. All of us know what happens when charges are made. If charges are made, the house has the opportunity of determining whether they should be submitted to a committee. And if any hon. member makes a charge he, of course, has to substantiate that charge, and if he fails to substantiate the charge the parliamentary tradition, indeed all the experience of the past, indicates that such a member having made a charge unconfirmed

and unsupported may be himself adjudged guilty of a breach of the privileges of the house.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier, when prime minister, in the House of Commons debates of 1907, at page 5664 of Hansard, with all his regard for the traditions of parliament and the necessity of their maintenance inviolate, made this statement that is most pertinent and applicable:
The house, I hope will not depart from the sound traditions which have come to us from England and according to which there could be no inquisition into any man's conduct or standing except on charges made specifically.

speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister arising out of conflicting press reports, one report stating that the Prime Minister had announced at Prince Albert that a Canadian satellite would be launched in 1961, and other reports attributing to certain defence research officials that the satellite would merely be a United States satellite with certain Canadian instruments attached to it. Can the Prime Minister tell the house just what is involved, and if this is to be in fact a Canadian satellite or merely a United States satellite to be launched from a Canadian base?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: REPORTED INTENTION TO LAUNCH CANADIAN SATELLITE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in so far as my statement at Prince Albert is concerned, it was in keeping with a joint announcement made in the month of April by Canada and the United States in connection with joint rocket vehicle and satellite experiments. I also dealt with the matter on another occasion.
In order to keep the record straight may I say that in so far as my remarks are concerned, and I repeat that they were in keeping with what had already been said on previous occasions, the background of the program is as follows. Canadian scientists

Inquiries of the Ministry are of the opinion that work on space research has now passed beyond the stage of hurling a satellite into space. They believe there is valuable scientific data on the properties of space that can be collected, analysed and considered.
Some time ago the defence research board and the defence research telecommunications establishment approached the appropriate United States authorities with proposals for a co-operative program of development in this field. In view of the fact that Canadian scientific personnel have the ability to make their contribution to the world's pool of knowledge in this field, we believe that Canadian technicians and scientists should be given that opportunity. They have proven themselves outstanding in conception, design and craftsmanship in the production of fine electronics components.
In so far as a satellite is concerned, the United States already has expensive and complex bases for launching earth satellites. It will be a considerable time, if ever, before it will be economic for Canada to establish her own satellite launching base. We do not believe that Canadian scientists should be held back on that account, and intend to give every possible encouragement to them to pursue this program and add to the collective pool of knowledge which can be turned to peaceful pursuits.
The purpose of launching satellites, as I have said, has now passed into the field of collecting valuable scientific data. The Canadian defence research telecommunications establishment at Shirley's bay is fully qualified to participate. When the satellite has finally been completed at D.R.T.E. it will be launched into a north-south polar orbit crossing the United States and Canada from the Vandenberg air force base in California, utilizing the multimillion dollar facilities I have already mentioned which are available there.
I mentioned that the launching would take place in 1961. I see some reference to the fact that this date has not been finally determined. The information I have received now is that it will not be launched earlier than 1961. With those explanations I think the hon. gentleman will understand the situation.

subsubtopic: REPORTED INTENTION TO LAUNCH CANADIAN SATELLITE
speechtext: Can the Prime Minister say how many Canadian technicians will be involved in this joint project, and whether the establishment of production facilities will result in substantial employment for Canadians? Will he also comment on the report in the press that Premier Frost has said that Moosonee is to be the launching site?

subsubtopic: REPORTED INTENTION TO LAUNCH CANADIAN SATELLITE
speechtext: I realize the obvious interest hon. gentlemen opposite have in the statements made by Premier Frost, but I have nothing to say with regard thereto. The general plans at the moment are that the launching will take place in the manner I have indicated. I am unable to give the hon. gentleman the details as to the numbers engaged, but I can say this. Canadians are engaged and are making a worth-while contribution to this highly desirable objective.

subsubtopic: REPORTED INTENTION TO LAUNCH CANADIAN SATELLITE
speechtext: In view of what the Prime Minister has said, will he explain exactly what he meant-and I quote from the text of his statement-when he said on Saturday "a Canadian satellite is to be launched in 1961"?

Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Transport. In view of the congestion and still further delays on the Welland canal,

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE SEAWAY WELLAND CANAL    SUGGESTED PRIORITIES FOR CANADIAN SHIPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to be able to assure the hon. member and other members of the house that the congestion at the Welland canal has now been, for all practical purposes, overcome. At nine o'clock this morning there were only four vessels waiting to enter the canal upbound at Port Weller and only four waiting to enter down-bound at Port Colborne.
As I have said on several occasions in this house, about three weeks ago I instituted a system of partial priorities by which vessels carrying bulk commodities would alternate with package freighters. This system of priorities was discussed in my office during a session lasting about one and one half hours with the presidents of several large Canadian shipping companies and the president of the Steel Company of Canada. At the conclusion of that meeting all were eminently satisfied with the system of priorities worked out. I hope the hon. member and other members of the house feel that the steps that were taken at that time have been successful. I sincerely hope, as I know he does, that the Welland canal will be able to continue to operate satisfactorily in the future without too much delay.

I would say that this is an exaggerated statement. I may say that the number of naval ships involved is 27, not 32. If the 27 naval ships were to present themselves up-bound over a period when the canal would have been otherwise fully engaged in transiting commercial vessels, the delay would possibly be the best part of two days. I am informed that the plans of the United States navy contemplate passage of 27 ships between June 23 and June 28 inclusive.
66968-9-280i
Inquiries of the Ministry It is not possible at this date to estimate accurately the result in delay to commercial vessels if this number of naval vessels have to be passed through in addition to the commercial traffic. At present the canal is handling both upbound and downbound traffic without appreciable delays; and as I have said, at nine o'clock this morning there were only four vessels awaiting entry at Port Colborne and four at Port Weller. subsubtopic: ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO IMPLEMENT PROMISES
speechtext:
So that I may relieve members on the treasury bench of any suspense they may

have in the matter, I can say that it is my intention before I resume my seat to move an amendment which in effect will ask the house to regret the failure of the government to implement promises made before the last two elections to the people of the Atlantic provinces.
I am sure this is one occasion when even with the greatest ingenuity-and I have no doubt that the greatest ingenuity will be employed in this case-it will be very difficult for the administration to get up, when I have completed, and say, "you did not do it; why didn't you do it?" I say this because the things about which I intend to speak this afternoon are things which the hon. gentlemen opposite, particularly their leader, promised and undertook to do; and because they are promises which, except in one or two cases where I will indicate the contrary, were not made by us and were not made by the federal government before 1959.
Thus there can be no question of any obligation on the part of the Liberal party or of the former Liberal government to undertake these things. Indeed, I am not sure that many Liberals would subscribe to all the promises that were made. But whether they would or not, the fact is that they were not made by Liberals and they were not made by the Liberal government and, as I intend to show in a moment or two, with one or two exceptions they have not been carried out, either.
